title: Amortized Cost-Effective Hallucination Mitigation via Uncertainty-Gated Sparse Ensembles: An A4 (Hierarchical Structure) Extension within the F-Theory Meta-Axiomatic Framework
abstract: This paper presents a Lean 4/Mathlib-verified framework in which ensemble-based hallucination mitigation is activated only when measured uncertainty exceeds a fixed threshold. Two theorems are proved: expected inference cost is always non-negative, and — critically — below the threshold, expected cost collapses exactly to the cost of a single base model, with zero residual ensemble overhead. The construction is framed as an A4 (Hierarchical Structure) extension of the author's F-Theory meta-axiomatic framework, giving a machine-checked guarantee that uncertainty-gated ensembling is cost-free outside the regime where hallucination risk is elevated.

title: Auditable by Construction: An Ontology-Driven Framework for Trustworthy LLM Analytics in Enterprise Finance — Reproducibility Artifact
abstract: This reproducibility artifact supports the preprint “Auditable by Construction: An Ontology-Driven Framework for Trustworthy LLM Analytics in Enterprise Finance.” It contains the code, configurations, ontology schema, prompts, identifier-only split manifest, aggregate and text-stripped results, environment records, and rebuild instructions for the reported 145-question, three-seed KDAF/CARP FinanceBench experiment. No FinanceBench questions, answers, justifications, evidence text, gold labels, or other benchmark prose are redistributed. Users must obtain FinanceBench separately from the upstream repository under its own terms. The included rebuild workflow fetches the pinned upstream files and verifies the evaluation, source-index, and graph digests before reproduction. FinanceBench citation: Islam, P., Kannappan, A., Kiela, D., Qian, R., Scherrer, N., and Vidgen, B. (2023). “FinanceBench: A New Benchmark for Financial Question Answering.” arXiv:2311.11944.

title: Computational Resonant Memory
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Resonant Memory (CRM), a fundamentally different approach to information storage and retrieval compared to traditional methods like databases and transformer caches. CRM posits that memory isn't about storing information, but rather about the *formation of resonant states*. The core principle is encapsulated in the Memory Resonance Equation, which describes the conditions under which a system transitions into and maintains a stable resonant state representing a stored memory. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of CRM, highlighting its potential to unify long-term memory mechanisms within a single computational framework. The central argument is that current memory architectures rely on discrete storage, while CRM leverages continuous resonant dynamics, offering a potentially more efficient and flexible approach to information representation and access. This paper lays the groundwork for future research into the design and implementation of CRM systems. ---

title: Algorithmic Transparency Classes
abstract: This paper introduces a hierarchical framework for classifying algorithmic transparency, moving beyond a binary "transparent" or "opaque" distinction. The proposed framework, termed "Algorithmic Transparency Classes," ( [T1, T2, ..., Tn] ) categorizes transparency based on distinct aspects of an algorithm: behavioral, state, decision, and mechanistic transparency. The core argument is that a complete understanding of transparency requires a layered approach, acknowledging that an algorithm may exhibit varying degrees of transparency across these categories. We explore a strict hierarchical relationship between these classes, aiming to provide a more nuanced and actionable approach to evaluating and improving algorithmic transparency. This framework offers a structured methodology for assessing the extent to which an algorithm's operation is understandable and explainable, with implications for accountability, trust, and responsible innovation in AI systems.

title: scmix: Bayesian Model-Based Clustering with Sparse Conditional Mixture Models
abstract: Fits Bayesian sparse conditional (Gaussian) mixture models for model-based clustering. Each mixture component factorizes into a chain of univariate polynomial regressions with per-component, per-equation Bayesian variable selection under a centered Zellner g-prior; the number of clusters is selected within a single run via an overfitted sparse mixture (Dirichlet concentration 1/K). The blocked Gibbs sampler draws the selection sets exactly by enumeration (or by validated single-flip Metropolis-Hastings in higher dimension), is provably well-posed under a documented proper fallback prior, and reports a label-invariant consensus partition (Dahl's least-squares criterion). Companion package to Dong, Liao, and Lee (2026), "Replacing three nested searches with one sweep: a Bayesian treatment of sparse conditional mixture clustering". Multiple-imputation functionality for the same engine is also exposed.

title: Risk-aware Model Learning for Robot Control
abstract: This thesis addresses the challenge of improving robot tracking accuracy when the available mathematical models are imperfect. We propose a framework that combines physics-based models with data-driven learning to bridge this gap. First, we develop a fast tracking controller that uses learned model updates while respecting robot torque limits. Second, we introduce a structured learning method that captures the physical properties of robot motion, ensuring more reliable predictions even with limited data. Finally, we propose a risk-aware strategy to collect informative data without exposing the robot to unpredictable movements. Together, these contributions enable robots to learn and improve safely.

title: LEXF-ATT-XLM: A hybrid lexicon-enhanced attention model for hate speech detection in low-resource language Roman Urdu
abstract: Hate speech detection in low-resource and informally written languages remains a significant challenge due to the lack of annotated corpora, orthographic variability, and complex code-mixing. Roman Urdu a non-standardized variant of Urdu written in the Latin script exemplifies these linguistic hurdles. In this paper, we propose LEXF-ATT-XLM, a novel hybrid deep learning architecture that synergizes contextual language modeling with explicit domain knowledge. Our model leverages XLM-RoBERTa for deep contextual embeddings, passed through a two-layer Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) and a multi-head attention mechanism to capture both sequential and salient linguistic patterns. Crucially, the pooled representations are fused via a learnable gating layer (Linear + tanh) before final classification. Furthermore, we integrate a domain specific Roman Urdu hate lexicon as an auxiliary regression supervision signal within a multi task learning framework to guide the model's focus. Evaluated on the RU-HSD-30K dataset using 3-fold stratified cross-validation, the proposed model achieves an average accuracy of 88.83% and a weighted F1 score of 88.83%, with fold wise weighted F1-scores of 88.58%, 89.19%, and 88.71%. Extensive ablation studies confirm that the lexicon-guided auxiliary supervision significantly enhances the model's ability to handle lexical variations, negations, and informal spelling. These findings demonstrate the robust effectiveness of our approach in addressing the unique linguistic challenges of Roman Urdu hate speech detection.

title: Feynman-Kac path integral extended Kalman filter with receding-horizon optimization for UAV-ASV landing mission
abstract: This study introduces an engineering integration framework with constraint-aware and anomaly-aware estimation capability, Receding Horizon Optimization Feynman-Kac Extended Kalman Filter (RHO-FK-EKF), designed to address the challenges of nonlinear disturbances, sensor anomalies, and malicious interference in high-dynamic inertial navigation environments for unmanned aerial vehicle and autonomous surface vessel (UAV-ASV). By integrating the Extended Kalman Filter, Support Vector Machine anomaly detection, receding-horizon optimization, Lagrange multiplier constraint handling, Bayesian recursive estimation, and Feynman-Kac path integrals, the proposed method achieves high precision and robustness in state estimation. Theoretical analysis establishes local convergence conditions for constrained optimization on differential manifolds, indicating that, under the linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ), system states remain confined to physically admissible manifolds. A stochastic-process-based derivation of the Feynman-Kac measure transformation confirms adaptability to non-Gaussian noise. Experimental evaluations, conducted under simulated shipborne landing scenarios, verify multi-level performance in filtering accuracy, constraint stability, interference rejection, and real-time responsiveness. The validation reported in this study combines numerical simulation, hardware-in-the-loop runs on the actual onboard processors, and engineering-level field tests using a VTOL UAV and an autonomous surface vessel platform. Results show that the proposed method maintains a positioning error within approximately ± 0.2 m, achieving a 60% improvement in accuracy over conventional techniques. During intentional interference, the anomaly detection system isolates attacks within 0.8 s and restores normal operation in 2.4 s. Under sea state level 4, the framework achieves a successful landing rate of approximately 96% on the present test set, significantly enhancing robustness in maritime operations. This research not only establishes an algorithmic integration for autonomous navigation but also provides rigorous mathematical and empirical foundations for reliable shipborne landings in non-radio-silent, high-risk environments.

title: Privacy‐Preserving Federated Audio‐Visual Saliency Analysis and Data Sharing Architecture for Rehabilitation of People With Disabilities
abstract: ABSTRACT Privacy constraints on facial, movement, and voice data restrict centralized model training across rehabilitation institutions. This study presents a privacy‐preserving federated audio‐visual saliency architecture, termed PPFAV, for edge‐based rehabilitation assessment. A three‐stream encoder represents speech instructions, dynamic action sequences, and static visual cues, while a self‐supervised cross‐modal alignment objective links synchronized instructions and movement responses. Before aggregation, clipped local updates are perturbed with calibrated Laplace noise so that raw samples remain at their local clients. Against the movement‐derived pseudo‐saliency references under the reported Non‐IID simulation, PPFAV achieved a correlation coefficient of 0.82 and a similarity score of 0.76, while retaining an F1‐score of 0.81 at = 0.1. These results indicate that cross‐modal alignment and privacy‐aware federated aggregation can support robust attention localization under simulated client heterogeneity. However, the evaluation is limited to a small controlled rehabilitation dataset with synthesized audio and simulated clients and networks; clinical validity, saliency‐ground‐truth reliability, and cumulative privacy accounting therefore require further verification.

title: Emergence of cooperation: A reputation-modulated reinforcement learning
abstract: Reputation is widely recognized as a key mechanism for sustaining cooperation. However, most existing game-theoretic models treat reputation primarily as an external factor that modulates payoffs, interaction structures, or strategy update rules. In many social contexts, though, reputation operates primarily as information -- it shapes how individuals interpret their own experiences and assess the behavior of others. To bridge this gap, we propose a spatial prisoner's dilemma game grounded in the reinforcement learning paradigm, in which agents equipped with Q-learning integrate both individual and social information via a locally defined reputation metric to guide their decisions. Our results reveal that reputation-modulated learning significantly promotes the emergence of cooperative behavior, and we observe a discontinuous phase transition from full cooperation to full defection as the temptation increases. Cooperation spreads through the nucleation of cooperative clusters, whereas the disintegration of these clusters drives the system into an absorbing state of complete defection. Overall, this study demonstrates that reputation facilitates cooperation not only by providing direct incentives but also by reshaping the social information landscape that agents rely on for learning and adaptation.

title: Computational Evaluation of FIFA Football AI Pro as a Generative AI Framework for Intelligent Football Performance Analytics
abstract: FIFA's Football AI Pro, developed with Official Technology Partner Lenovo and deployed at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, is a generative artificial intelligence assistant built on a domain-specific Football Language Model and provided to all 48 competing national teams. This paper presents a computational evaluation of Football AI Pro based on publicly disclosed technical and operational information, since no independent access to the system or its training data is currently available. A structured evaluation framework is applied across six dimensions: data scale and coverage, architectural sophistication, explainability, accessibility, operational risk controls and data governance transparency. The evaluation suggests that the platform is credible mainly because it uses FIFA's large proprietary dataset. This dataset is larger and more consistent than those used in most football machine learning research. However, there is no independent evidence to confirm its explainability and governance claims. The paper concludes that Football AI Pro is a reliable and well-developed generative AI platform for sports analytics. However, its evaluation is based mainly on claims made by the company, not on independent technical testing. Keywords: generative AI; large language models; Sports Analytics; FIFA; Football AI Pro; computational evaluation

title: Основни принципи и философски аспекти на невросимволния изкуствен интелект
abstract: The present article aims to examine the main factors that have led to the emergence of hybrid approaches in the field of artificial intelligence and mainly of neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence. It is primarily concerned with clarifying and analyzing its principles and fundamental characteristics and their role in obtaining reliable knowledge. At the same time, the article outlines and discusses several philosophical questions and proposes some interpretations related to its nature and development. One of the proposed hypotheses in the paper is that neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence, on the one hand, possesses the capacity to come very close to achieving artificial general intelligence and, on the other hand, has the potential to prevent such an outcome, which depends on the objectives and moral values embedded in the design and implementation of a particular neuro-symbolic AI system.

title: Security and privacy challenges of RAG systems
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enable robust knowledge integration for large language models but also pose significant security and privacy risks. RAG systems combine two components: a retriever, which searches external data sources for relevant information, and a generator, typically a large language model that uses both the retrieved documents and user queries to produce answers. This study conducts a systematic literature review to assess these challenges using Socio-Technical Systems Theory (which considers interactions among people, technology, and organizational context) and Privacy by Design (PbD, a framework for embedding privacy into system design). Addressing five objectives, the research detects and classifies privacy attacks, evaluates risks throughout the storage, retrieval, and generation phases, scrutinizes measurement methods, contrasts mitigation strategies, and introduces a unified solution. The work culminates in the Integrated Privacy-Preserving RAG Framework (IPRAG), a five-tier architecture supported by a three-phase deployment protocol. This study presents a detailed, actionable approach to constructing secure, privacy-focused RAG systems.

Addressing five objectives, the research detects and classifies privacy attacks, evaluates risks throughout the storage, retrieval, and generation phases, scrutinizes measurement methods, contrasts mitigation strategies, and introduces a unified solution. The work culminates in the Integrated Privacy-Preserving RAG Framework (IPRAG), a five-tier architecture supported by a three-phase deployment protocol. This study presents a detailed, actionable approach to constructing secure, privacy-focused RAG systems.

title: Computational Substitutability Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Substitutability Theory (CST), a novel framework for analyzing the degree to which a computational component (Ci) can be replaced within a broader computational process (C). The core concept is defined as S(Ci | C), representing the extent of substitution. This theory provides a quantitative approach to understanding dependencies and redundancies within complex computational systems, offering insights for optimization, resilience, and efficient resource allocation. The theory is presented with a formal definition and explores key implications for various domains, including software engineering, distributed computing, and artificial intelligence. This work lays the foundation for a systematic methodology to assess and manage computational substitutability, ultimately leading to more robust and adaptable systems. The central question addressed is: How replaceable is a computation? ---

title: Numerical Simulations for Environmental Impacts
abstract: Abstract: Numerical simulation has become an indispensable tool in environmental impact assessments (EIA) given the increasing complexity and interconnection among natural systems. In this chapter we explore how the R programming language can serve as a platform for developing and analysing simulations representing different environmental processes. We discuss atmospheric pollutant dispersion using Gaussian plume models, soil nitrogen dynamics and nitrate leaching within agro-ecosystems, and ecological responses to climate change through differential-equation and multivariate statistical models. Instead of providing implementation code, the focus is on highlighting conceptual designs using core R packages such as deSolve, EnvStats and ggplot2 and then discussing the resultant simulation outcomes. While R offers great potential in providing actionable insights into environmental processes by enabling pollutant concentration, nutrient flux, and ecosystem dynamics simulations, there are challenges related to parameter uncertainty, multiscale integration, and computational demands. Finally, we suggest that hybrid programming approaches, deeper integration with remote sensing data, and unification under common, cross-disciplinary modelling frameworks will define the next phase of environmental simulations in R. Keywords: Numerical Simulation, Environmental Modeling, R Programming, Gaussian Plume Model, Climate Change Impact

title: Mathematical Theorem Fertility
abstract: The concept of theorem fertility is introduced as a quantitative framework for evaluating the generative power of mathematical theorems. A theorem's fertility, denoted Fert(P), is defined as the potential of theorem P to serve as a starting point for the derivation of other theorems within a formal system. This paper develops the theoretical foundations of theorem fertility, establishes key properties such as additivity and subadditivity, and explores the relationship between fertility and proof complexity. We formalize the notion of fertility for compound theorems and prove that, under standard axiomatic assumptions, Fert(P ∧ Q) is generally not equal to Fert(P) + Fert(Q) but satisfies a weak subadditivity inequality. Several illustrative examples from elementary number theory and algebra demonstrate how fertility can be computed and used to compare the generative capacities of different theorems. We further discuss the implications of theorem fertility for automated theorem proving and mathematical discovery, proposing fertility as a guiding metric for prioritizing conjectures in proof search. The paper concludes with open questions about the interaction between fertility and logical strength, and suggests directions for future research.

title: Computational Ambiguity Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Ambiguity Theory (CAT), a novel framework for analyzing and quantifying ambiguity within computational systems. Unlike traditional approaches that primarily focus on resolving ambiguity through single, definitive interpretations, CAT posits that a single input can support a multitude of legitimate computational interpretations. This theory is founded on the principle that ambiguity isn't a deficiency, but rather a rich source of potential computational pathways. The theory leverages concepts from information theory, set theory, and logic to formally define and measure the 'computational ambiguity space' associated with a given input. Key elements of the theory include the definition of 'computational interpretations' (CI), the identification of 'computational pathways' (CP), and the quantification of 'interpretational diversity' (ID). We explore the implications of CAT across several domains, including AI reasoning, program analysis, and natural language processing. The core mathematical formulation is presented, focusing on the relationship between input complexity, the number of CIs, and the overall ID. The theory provides a rigorous methodology for assessing ambiguity levels, ultimately aiming to improve the robustness and adaptability of computational systems. Furthermore, we outline potential extensions and future research directions, highlighting the potential of CAT to reshape our understanding of ambiguity in the digital age.

title: Algorithmic Necessity Extraction
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Algorithmic Necessity Extraction (ANE), a novel approach to identifying the core computational structures fundamentally required for a given algorithm to function. Unlike traditional techniques like code compression or model pruning, ANE aims to establish a formal necessity proof, resulting in a minimal computational structure – (P*) – that guarantees the algorithm's continued operation. The goal is to shift the focus from simply reducing code size to understanding the absolute essential components. The process involves defining a set of potential computational structures, [P], and then iteratively refining this set based on a necessity criterion. The resulting (P*) represents a mathematically rigorous justification for the algorithm's core design, potentially leading to new insights and a revised understanding of program theory. This work presents a theoretical framework and outlines the key components needed to implement ANE, focusing on the identification of the minimal structure required for algorithmic execution.

title: Executable explanation traces for legal LLM predictions via retrieval-augmented codification
abstract: Explainability is particularly challenging in legal prediction, where decisions are expected not only to be accurate but also to be justified under explicit legal norms and open to external scrutiny. Legal reasoning therefore provides one of the most demanding settings for explainable AI because a legal determination often depends on information distributed across the input record, external legal sources, procedural context, evidentiary assumptions, and institutional judgment. Direct outcome generation hides this decision path, while natural-language rationales and retrieved citations do not necessarily show whether a legal condition was actually applied. This article presents studies of retrieval-augmented codification as a way to produce executable explanation traces for legal large language model (LLM) predictions. The goal is not to generate human-facing rationales directly, but to produce auditable artifacts: short programs that extract signals, apply program-level conditions, follow branches, and produce final labels under a fixed output schema. The approach retrieves legal sources and fold-safe in-domain examples, compiles them into an executable intermediate representation, and refines the program using model feedback. The resulting trace records retrieved materials, generated conditions, feedback, and the final prediction. We evaluate this framework on five legal benchmarks covering Chinese criminal law, European human-rights cases, U.S. class-action complaints, Indian judgments, and Japanese tort cases. The evaluation asks not only whether the predicted label is correct, but also whether the explanation is executable, whether its conditions are supported by retrieved legal sources, whether it responds to legally material edits, and where it fails. The results show that executable explanations can be obtained without sacrificing predictive utility: the full codification setting improves mean label accuracy over direct prompting, chain-of-thought prompting, one-pass codification, and text-based retrieval baselines. More importantly, trace analysis reveals why legal explainability is difficult. Codification is most informative when decisions depend on definitions, thresholds, exceptions, and other rule-like components. It is less complete when benchmark labels depend on procedural, evidentiary, or discretionary factors outside the input record. These findings position retrieval-augmented codification as a practical explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) tool for studying when legal LLM predictions can be explained through explicit, source-supported decision paths.

title: Question-Guided Evidence Acquisition for Multimodal Visual Question Answering
abstract: Multimodal LLMs can see a document, but they often can't read it reliably. Small text, tables, visual cues, and topological elements still trip them up under direct visual inference, even when the page is already sitting in the model's context. Most document-VQA systems treat perception as fixed: they encode the page once, ask the question, and answer from whatever the model happened to extract in that single fast pass. We think document VQA needs slower, more deliberate perception: rather than answering from one fixed encoding, the model should spend a bit of extra compute at inference time working out what to look at next, and only then answer. We build this into \textbf{Q-Guide}, a small agent that reads a question, works out what evidence it is still missing, and calls targeted tool(s) to recover it---reading text where text is needed, zooming in where detail is needed, or grounding a region where position matters. On DocVQA2026 and Manga109, Q-Guide outperforms both direct prompting and recent multi-agent document systems ($65.0\%$ vs.\ $40.0\%$ on DocVQA2026, $32.4\%$ vs.\ $24.4\%$ on Manga109), and the improvement holds across three Claude backbones (Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, and Opus 4.5). We find that accuracy scales with the perception budget---most of the gain appears within two to three deliberate rounds---and that the gain comes from directing perception to the right place, not from complex control logic: adding planners, routers, or multiple collaborating agents does not help.

title: SDKB — Semiconductor Domain Knowledge Base (paper release)
abstract: SDKB is a provenance-grounded semiconductor domain ontology dataset carrying expert matching, prior-art search and technology foresight as task views on one shared schema (T-Box). This release is the frozen state accompanying the SDKB prior-art paper. Contents. Shared T-Box and task views (OWL/TTL), SHACL shapes, 31 competency questions, concept mappings, provenance records with per-file SHA-256 for all published assets, and benchmark/ — the evaluation harness (retrieval systems, release-gate conditions, scoring and statistics) together with frozen evaluation assets: query and relevance-judgment identifiers, split boundaries, frozen thresholds, gate reports, fault-injection matrices and result tables. Licensing. This deposit is dual-licensed and therefore does not map to a single identifier. Data layers (ontology, mappings, validation shapes, queries, provenance) are released under CDLA-Permissive-2.0; code (generators, release chain, evaluation harness) is released under Apache-2.0; documentation under CC-BY-4.0. See LICENSE.txt and LICENSE-CODE.txt in the archive. Not included. Patent full text is not redistributable under the terms of the source database; identifiers and a refetch procedure are provided instead. Known reproduction limits are stated in benchmark/README.md.

title: Computational Potential
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of "Computational Potential" (CP), a novel metric designed to assess the future viability and value embedded within a given state or situation. Unlike traditional utility measures, which focus on immediate satisfaction or benefit, CP specifically quantifies the inherent capacity for a state to generate further computational advancement or value over time. The core principle posits that a state's CP is determined by its potential to transition into a more favorable state, with the magnitude of this potential represented by the difference in computational capability between the initial and subsequent states. This framework allows for a nuanced understanding of long-term strategic value, moving beyond purely present-centric considerations. The paper outlines the fundamental definition of CP and explores scenarios where CP increases or decreases, highlighting the dynamic nature of this concept.

title: Algorithmic Order Invariant
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of an algorithmic order invariant, a property that transcends the specific implementation details of two algorithms. Two algorithms, denoted as [A, B], can perform vastly different operations at a low level, utilizing diverse data structures and computational techniques. However, if these algorithms exhibit a shared fundamental order structure, represented as [ \mathcal{O}(A) \cong \mathcal{O}(B) ], the paper defines a new invariant, I_O(A) = I_O(B). This invariant suggests that the inherent order within the algorithms is what truly matters, independent of the specific methods employed to achieve that order. The paper explores the theoretical implications of this concept, focusing on identifying and characterizing algorithms that possess this inherent order structure. The core argument rests on the observation that many algorithms, particularly those dealing with sorting and searching, rely on underlying ordering principles, and that these principles can be abstracted and compared, leading to a robust and quantifiable measure of algorithmic similarity. This work lays the groundwork for a novel approach to algorithm analysis, shifting the focus from implementation details to the fundamental order relationships within algorithms.

title: Algorithmic Dependency Types
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Algorithmic Dependency Types (ADTs), a formal framework for categorizing and ordering relationships between algorithms. We define five primary types of dependencies: value dependency (D_v), existence dependency (D_e), order dependency (D_o), state dependency (D_s), and history dependency (D_h). The core of the research investigates whether a strict partial order can be established between these ADT types. This work lays a foundational structure for understanding and reasoning about complex algorithmic interactions, offering a potential basis for automated verification and optimization techniques. The paper presents a detailed definition of each dependency type, followed by a rigorous analysis of their relationships. The ultimate goal is to provide a systematic approach to managing and controlling dependencies within software systems and algorithmic processes. ---

title: Algorithmic Vacancy Transition
abstract: This paper investigates the phenomenon of "Algorithmic Vacancy Transition," proposing a novel framework for understanding the dynamic relationship between structural deficiencies (vacancies) within algorithmic systems and the subsequent emergence of innovative solutions. The core hypothesis centers on the idea that when a gap or void exists within an algorithm—represented as a 'vacancy'—a predictable process of innovation will occur to fill it. We explore the potential for a universal rule governing this transition, suggesting it could represent a significant component of theoretical algorithmic discovery. This research moves beyond simply observing innovation to establishing a mechanistic link between algorithmic gaps and the generation of new algorithms, focusing on the inherent drive toward optimization and the exploration of alternative pathways. The study employs a conceptual framework, outlining key parameters and potential mathematical representations of this transition, and identifies areas for future research to validate these hypotheses. ---

title: Information Ownership Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Information Ownership Theory (IOT), a framework for understanding the complex evolution of ownership rights associated with information assets undergoing transformation. Traditional intellectual property law struggles to adequately address information that has been subjected to processes such as replication, compression, training, and dissemination – hallmarks of the digital age. IOT proposes that information ownership is not solely determined by its initial creation but is fundamentally shaped by the 'Ownership State' – a dynamic concept encompassing the various factors influencing rights control throughout the information lifecycle. This theory directly addresses implications for AI copyright and data governance, arguing for a more nuanced approach that considers the cumulative impact of these transformative processes. The core of the theory rests on the following key elements: (1) the identification and quantification of 'Ownership State' variables, (2) the development of mathematical models to predict ownership shifts based on these variables, and (3) the application of these models to assess the ownership implications of various information processing activities. This paper outlines the foundational principles of IOT and proposes a methodology for its further development and application. ---

title: CMS-Attack: A Structured Cross-Modal Search Attack for Robustness Evaluation of LiDAR–Camera Fusion Detectors
abstract: LiDAR-camera fusion is widely used for 3D perception in intelligent connected vehicles, but a clean camera branch does not necessarily compensate for structured LiDAR corruption. We propose CMS-Attack, a cross-modal search framework in which only the LiDAR point cloud is perturbed while the camera input remains unchanged; here, "cross-modal" denotes that a single-modality LiDAR perturbation propagates through the LiDAR-camera fusion process and disrupts the multimodal detector, rather than simultaneous perturbation of both modalities. The framework has the following two access-dependent routes: the gray-box route contains FB-CMS, which uses camera-BEV, LiDAR-BEV, fused-BEV, and detection-head responses to construct a target-aware prior and prune an over-complete candidate pool, and Adaptive CMS, which substitutes architecture-specific intermediate responses; the decision-only black-box route contains FC-CMS, which refines candidates solely from display-level target states. On the nuScenes validation split, FB-CMS reduced matched target confidence from 0.80 to 0.03 under 140 injected points, corresponding to a 96.1% relative drop and 100% ASR@0.3. The ten-query FC-CMS achieved 58.97% ASR@0.3, compared with 6.17% for random frustum spoofing. On the query-based FUTR3D detector, Adaptive CMS reduced the mean matched-target score from 0.642 to 0.058, corresponding to a 90.97% relative reduction and 93.42% ASR@0.3. Intermediate camera-, LiDAR-, and fused-BEV region energies changed by less than 0.8% despite target suppression, indicating disruption at the fusion-decision stage (defined here as the decoder/detection-head and post-processing path from fused representations to final object predictions) rather than a collapse of BEV feature magnitude. These results show that structured LiDAR fabrication is substantially more disruptive than information removal and that generic outlier filtering incurs a robustness-accuracy tradeoff.

title: G-CARL: Grounded Checklist-Aligned Reward Learning for Patient-Oriented Medical Report Interpretation
abstract: Personalized interpretation of medical reports has emerged as an increasingly important need among patients. Addressing this need requires both evidence-grounded medical factuality and context-dependent patient communication, yet existing medical vision-language tasks do not adequately capture these dual requirements. To bridge this gap, we introduce Patient-oriented Medical Report Interpretation (PMRI), a novel open-ended multimodal generation task that requires models to explain medical reports in accurate and accessible language based on a user's query and dialogue history. These two objectives differ fundamentally in their verifiability, yet remain tightly coupled, making them difficult to optimize jointly under conventional supervised fine-tuning and holistic reinforcement learning paradigms. To address this challenge, we propose G-CARL, a grounded, checklist-aligned reinforcement learning framework that combines multi-source retrieval for atomic claim verification with context-aware, instance-specific weighted checklists for response coverage, providing structured supervision for factuality, user-demand satisfaction, and expression quality without constraining response diversity. We further construct MMedReport, a real-world PMRI benchmark, along with a clinician-designed three-dimensional evaluation protocol. Extensive experiments demonstrate that G-CARL consistently outperforms existing post-training baselines in overall quality, claim-level precision, and checklist recall. Pairwise preference evaluation by clinicians further confirms that G-CARL produces interpretations that are more accurate and better aligned with patient needs.

title: Learning to Beat: Phenotype-Guided Latent Flow with Regional Motion Priors for Biventricular Motion Synthesis
abstract: Full-cycle biventricular geometry is essential for characterizing cardiac function. However, dense and temporally consistent 3D+t biventricular meshes are not routinely available, whereas end-diastolic (ED) anatomy can often be obtained reliably. We therefore investigate full-cycle biventricular motion synthesis from a single ED mesh. This task is challenging because cardiac deformation is spatially heterogeneous and phenotype dependent, while conventional global generative models often obscure localized motion patterns. In this study, we propose a region-specific and phenotype-adaptive framework that integrates motion-informed functional parcellation with conditional latent flow. A functional partition learned from reconstructed motion organizes the ventricular surface into regions with coherent dynamics and enables topology-aware regional feature exchange. A phenotype-conditioned rectified-flow model subsequently maps the ED anatomy to full-cycle motion latents through fine-grained conditioning and prototype-routed motion adapters. An optional control branch further incorporates available motion descriptors for controllable synthesis. Experiments on ACDC, M\&Ms, and M\&Ms-2 demonstrate consistent improvements in geometric accuracy and functional fidelity. Under ED-only synthesis, our method achieves biventricular ASSD, HD95, and vRMSE of \(1.49\pm0.34\)~mm, \(3.77\pm1.06\)~mm, and \(3.31\pm1.03\)~mm, respectively, outperforming all competing methods. Complementary functional and robustness evaluations further demonstrate that the synthesized sequences preserve physiologically plausible ventricular dynamics and generalize across cohorts and disease phenotypes. The code will be released publicly upon acceptance of the manuscript for publication.

title: A Nine-Dimensional Ternary Cognitive Architecture for Autonomous Financial Agents: From Philosophical Foundations to Geometric Implementation
abstract: Financial AI systems today operate on a hidden axiom: that every decision reduces to a binary choice. This paper presents Aether-HexQ, a cognitive architecture for autonomous financial agents built on balanced ternary trits (+1/0/-1), where the neutral state (0) is formally recognized as a legitimate cognitive condition representing uncertainty. The architecture integrates balanced ternary logic, symplectic geometry, pi-e coupled dynamics, and multi-agent federation into a unified framework for autonomous financial decision-making.

title: Realization Distance
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of realization distance, a metric designed to quantify the difference between two implementations of the same function. The core idea revolves around defining a space, denoted as $(\mathcal{I}(f), d_{\mathrm{impl}})$ where $\mathcal{I}(f)$ represents the set of all possible implementations of a function *f*, and $d_{\mathrm{impl}}$ represents the realization distance between two implementations. The distance, $d_{\mathrm{impl}}(P, Q)$, is defined as the minimum number of legal transformations required to transform implementation *P* into implementation *Q*. This research explores the fundamental properties of this distance metric and its potential applications in areas such as program analysis, compiler optimization, and formal verification. The paper lays the groundwork for a more rigorous study of implementation equivalence and the challenges associated with comparing different software representations. The central question addressed is: "How far apart can two implementations of the same function be?"

title: AI avatars in education: effects on knowledge acquisition, academic motivation, and cognitive load
abstract: As digital learning environments increasingly incorporate artificial intelligence, empirical evidence regarding the educational effectiveness of AI-powered digital avatars remains limited and methodologically heterogeneous. This randomized matched-pair study examined whether learning with a human-like AI-avatar instructional system implemented in Unity 3D with Convai and OpenAI GPT-4o for real-time verbal interaction improves knowledge acquisition, academic motivation, and perceived cognitive load compared with autonomous internet-based learning. Forty-eight university students were included in the final analytic sample and were balanced across instructional condition and gender (AI-avatar: n = 24; control: n = 24; 12 males and 12 females in each condition). Participants completed an instructional task on introductory artificial intelligence and neural-network concepts, followed by a 20-item knowledge test, the Academic Motivation Scale, and a shortened Cognitive Load Scale. Separate 2 x 2 analyses of variance tested the effects of instructional condition and gender for each dependent variable. Reliability was satisfactory for the Academic Motivation Scale (pre-test Cronbach's α = 0.88; post-test α = 0.97) and the Cognitive Load Scale ( α =.77). The AI-avatar group obtained higher knowledge-test scores than the control group ( M = 10.63, SD = 2.39 vs. M = 8.92, SD = 3.11), F (1, 44) = 4.66, p = 0.036, partial η 2 = 0.096. Academic motivation showed a more favorable pre-to-post trajectory in the AI-avatar condition (ΔSDI M = −1.15, SD = 3.67) than in the control condition (ΔSDI M = −4.36, SD = 3.70), F (1, 44) = 9.22, p = 0.004, partial η 2 = 0.173; the unadjusted post-test SDI condition effect approached significance ( p = 0.051), and an ANCOVA controlling for baseline motivation was significant ( p = 0.006). Perceived cognitive load did not differ significantly between conditions, F (1, 44) = 0.16, p = 0.688. No significant gender main effects or condition-by-gender interactions emerged for the main outcomes. These findings suggest that AI-avatar-supported instruction may enhance knowledge acquisition and support motivational regulation, while evidence for cognitive-load reduction was not observed in the present data. The novelty of the study lies in its direct empirical comparison of next-generation, human-like AI-avatar learning support with conventional self-directed online learning, while also reporting outcome-specific analyses and limitations relevant to reproducibility.

title: Algorithmic Cost in "Exact Real Computation"
abstract: Turing completeness of a programming language or system characterizes its expressive power; and the strong Church-Turing hypo-/thesis refines such from qualitative to polynomial-time equivalence. Exact Real Computation (ERC) is a novel numerical programming language paradigm: for the imperative processing of continuous data as entities appearing as exact, i.e. devoid of rounding errors [doi:10.1007/978-3-662-44199-2_107]. ERC has been designed [doi:10.46298/lmcs-20(2:17)2024] as convenient and practical alternative, namely proven qualitatively equivalent, to the Turing machines originally underlying Computable Analysis [doi:10.1007/978-3-642-56999-9,doi:10.1007/978-1-4684-6802-1]. The present work quantitatively strengthens this qualitative Turing-completeness: We assign bit-costs to ERC's operational primitives (including partial/multivalued tests) in such a way that any real function incurring polynomial cost becomes Turing-computable in polynomial time, and vice versa. Runtime measurements on implementations in the iRRAM C++ library confirm our theoretical performance predictions.

evidence.title: Algorithmic Cost in "Exact Real Computation"
evidence.abstract: Turing completeness of a programming language or system characterizes its expressive power; and the strong Church-Turing hypo-/thesis refines such from qualitative to polynomial-time equivalence. Exact Real Computation (ERC) is a novel numerical programming language paradigm: for the imperative processing of continuous data as entities appearing as exact, i.e. devoid of rounding errors [doi:10.1007/978-3-662-44199-2_107]. ERC has been designed [doi:10.46298/lmcs-20(2:17)2024] as convenient and practical alternative, namely proven qualitatively equivalent, to the Turing machines originally underlying Computable Analysis [doi:10.1007/978-3-642-56999-9,doi:10.1007/978-1-4684-6802-1]. The present work quantitatively strengthens this qualitative Turing-completeness: We assign bit-costs to ERC's operational primitives (including partial/multivalued tests) in such a way that any real function incurring polynomial cost becomes Turing-computable in polynomial time, and vice versa. Runtime measurements on implementations in the iRRAM C++ library confirm our theoretical performance predictions.

title: $TCP_α$: Margin-Controlled Confidence estimation for reliable Music Information Retrieval
abstract: Deep neural networks are often overconfident, assigning high confidence even to incorrect predictions. Consequently, users lack a reliable signal for deciding when a prediction can be trusted. Post-hoc confidence estimation addresses this by training a lightweight auxiliary head over a frozen classifier. Existing targets, however, suffer from inherent ambiguity: they assign overlapping confidence values to correct and incorrect predictions, while errors near the decision boundary receive confidence scores indistinguishable from correct predictions. In this work, we propose $TCP_α$, a novel confidence target that resolves these limitations by introducing a margin-controlled penalty for misclassified samples. We prove that $TCP_α$ guarantees complete separation between the target values of correct and incorrect predictions, with a separation margin that is independent of the number of classes and increases monotonically with the penalty parameter. Since accurate classifiers naturally produce very few errors, learning these targets results in a severely imbalanced regression problem. We therefore present a systematic study of training strategies for learning under this imbalance and identify an effective training configuration through extensive ablation studies. We evaluate the proposed approach on rāga identification, investigate its robustness under domain shift, and further validate it on frame-wise ornamentation detection without modifying the selected configuration. Across all settings, $TCP_α$ consistently outperforms existing confidence targets for failure prediction. Rejecting only the least-confident 8\% of predictions improves the base model's macro-F1 from 0.89 to 0.98, while fine-tuning the confidence head with only 5\% labeled samples from a new corpus effectively restores performance under domain shift.

title: Scale-Aware Pretraining of Time Series Foundation Models via Multi-Patch Token Alignment and Hybrid Masking
abstract: Pretraining time series foundation models across heterogeneous datasets necessitates effective handling of varying sampling frequencies. Current methods either employ dataset-specific patch sizes and separate FFNs, leading to fragmented representations, or enforce a fixed patch size that neglects inherent temporal variations. To address this, we propose SATS, featuring a scale-aware token alignment mechanism that treats patch size as an explicit notion of scale. By incorporating a contrastive-inspired alignment regularizer, SATS aligns representation spaces across scales while preserving distinct modeling capacities. Furthermore, a hybrid masking strategy combining random and contiguous masking is introduced to capture multi-scale temporal structures. Experimental results on LSTF benchmarks demonstrate that SATS achieves a 9.2% improvement in MSE and an 8.3% gain in GIFT-Eval MASE compared to competitive baselines. Notably, SATS consistently delivers SOTA performance while achieving a 65.6% increase in model efficiency over advanced baselines, highlighting its effectiveness and scalability in time series pretraining.

title: Distilling Normalizing Flows for Real-Time Anomaly Detection at the LHC
abstract: Normalizing flows are principled anomaly detectors, selecting anomalies using a probabilistic per-event likelihood. Extreme latency and resource constraints have prevented the deployment of flow likelihoods within the hardware triggers at the Large Hadron Collider. We bypass these limitations by distilling the likelihood from a large normalizing flow into lightweight student estimators suitable for deployment on a field-programmable gate array. Our use of a conditional normalizing flow enables precise likelihood estimation in the presence of missing input features. Both decision tree and neural network students are considered, the latter optimized under advanced quantization techniques. By simultaneously improving likelihood quality and lowering inference cost, we demonstrate both state-of-the-art physics performance and latency compared with existing flow-based approaches.

title: cryptoflex: A Local-First Crypto-Agility Policy Engine for HybridClassical and Post-Quantum Key Exchange
abstract: The transition from classical to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) presentsacritical challenge for software systems that rely on hardcoded algorithmicchoices. Most encryption tools select a single cryptographic stack at buildtimeand never revisit that decision, creating a maintainability and security liabilityas algorithms are deprecated or broken. While large-scale network protocolssuch as Signal’s PQXDH and Chrome’s X25519Kyber768 have alreadyshipped hybrid classical+PQC key exchange, the local-first domain —fileencryption utilities, desktop applications, and embedded/IoT systems —remains underserved. This paper presents cryptoflex, a local-first crypto-agility policy engine forPython that orchestrates existing, independently audited cryptographicprimitives behind a runtime decision layer. The system combines classicalX25519 elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman with NIST-standardized Module-Lattice- Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) via the Open QuantumSafe(liboqs) library. A versioned, bundled risk table enables algorithmdeprecationwithout network dependency. A deterministic hybrid combiner binds all sharedsecrets and ciphertexts into a single 256-bit root key via HKDF-SHA384, achieving the standard “at-least-as-strong-as-the-strongest-component” security property. The system is validated through a comprehensive test suitecovering policy degradation, combiner correctness, and header serializationround-trips

title: Reason Interference
abstract: This paper investigates the phenomenon of "Reason Interference," a situation where two independent and correct computational justifications, when considered together, lead to a contradictory result. We formalize this interference through the introduction of the index *IR(r1, r2)*, where *r1* and *r2* represent the two computational reasons. The core concept is that while *r1* and *r2* individually yield a specific outcome *y*, their combined presence results in a modified outcome *y'*. This paper establishes a foundational framework for understanding and analyzing situations where the convergence of logical arguments can introduce unexpected and disruptive changes in conclusions. The analysis focuses on the interplay between individual justifications and the resultant alteration of the overall outcome, highlighting the potential for conflict within seemingly sound reasoning processes.

title: From Equations to Intelligence: The Evolution of Mathematics in the Era of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Abstract: Mathematics has long been recognized as the universal language of science, providing systematic approaches for describing natural phenomena through logical reasoning and quantitative analysis. Over time, mathematical sciences have evolved beyond traditional analytical methods, integrating statistical reasoning, computational techniques, and data-driven methodologies to address increasingly complex real-world challenges. This evolution has given rise to Data Science, Machine Learning, and Artificial Intelligence, transforming the way knowledge is generated, and decisions are made across scientific, engineering, and social domains. This chapter traces the intellectual journey from classical mathematical formulations to modern intelligent computational systems. It discusses how mathematical concepts such as linear algebra, calculus, probability, optimization, and numerical methods underpin contemporary machine learning algorithms and artificial intelligence. The chapter further highlights interdisciplinary applications, emerging research trends, and future opportunities where mathematical thinking continues to drive innovation. By presenting mathematics as an evolving discipline rather than a static body of knowledge, the chapter emphasizes its enduring relevance in shaping the next generation of intelligent technologies.

title: Algorithmic Opportunity Window
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of the "Algorithmic Opportunity Window" (AOW), a novel framework for understanding and optimizing algorithmic performance. It argues that algorithmic capability is not solely determined by inherent potential, but crucially depends on the temporal availability of that capability – the existence of an AOW. The AOW is defined as a finite period during which a specific algorithmic function or process is both capable and appropriately triggered. The paper explores various types of AOWs, including those associated with reasoning, search, communication, and learning processes. It posits that system design should not only focus on 'what' an algorithm *can* do, but equally importantly, 'when' it can effectively utilize that capacity. This perspective offers a new lens for analyzing resource allocation, scheduling, and overall system efficiency within dynamic computational environments. The framework provides a foundation for developing adaptive systems that intelligently manage opportunity windows to maximize algorithmic effectiveness. ---

title: Computational Adaptation Limit
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of the Computational Adaptation Limit (CAL), proposing that the maximum adaptability of any intelligent system is fundamentally constrained by its structural architecture, rather than solely by computational resources. The argument centers on the observation that intelligent systems, despite potentially vast computational power, often exhibit limitations in their ability to effectively adapt to novel environments or tasks. We introduce the term "Adaptation Ceiling" to describe this limit. The paper explores the theoretical underpinnings of CAL, examining how architectural bottlenecks—such as the sequential nature of processing, inherent biases within algorithms, and the limitations of feedback loops—restrict the system's capacity to truly adapt. We outline a framework for understanding CAL, suggesting that a deeper investigation of system design, rather than simply increasing processing power, is crucial for achieving genuine adaptability in artificial intelligence. The core premise is that efficient adaptation requires a system's structure to be intrinsically aligned with the demands of the environment, a requirement frequently overlooked in current approaches. This paper lays the groundwork for a new perspective on AI development, emphasizing architectural constraints as a primary factor in determining adaptive potential.

title: AI-Driven Innovations in Sustainable Tourism Marketing
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the future of sustainable tourism marketing, and with it offers a degree of potential on hyper-personalization, predictive analytics, and responsible management of resources such as has not been seen before. This chapter examines how AI can be used in a multidimensional context to advance sustainability objectives in the tourism sector. The paper looks at utilization scenarios of AI-based recommendation engines to promote carbon-neutral itineraries, to applications of generative AI that can support awe-inspiring eco-branding material. The chapter. sets besides research in consumer behavioural reactions to AI-mediated sustainable travel publicity, and in addition evaluates the ethical implications of the usage of the technologies including the possibility of information privacy violation, algorithm favouritism and the environmental cost of the AI infrastructure itself. Through the UN SDGs, the analysis suggests a combined approach to the ethical aspects of the implementation of the artificial intelligence in tourism marketing.

title: Understanding the Basics
abstract: In this chapter, we introduce some fundamental concepts and tools that are essential for statistical consulting. We begin with an introduction to the R software, which is widely used for data analysis and visualization, followed by a brief overview of a typical workflow in R. We then discuss the fundamentals of data, including common data types, formats, and manipulations. Next, we cover the basics of data visualization, highlighting commonly used plots for exploratory data analysis. Finally, we review some fundamental statistical concepts, including common parametric distributions, descriptive statistics, and how to choose appropriate statistical methods based on data types and research questions in a general sense.

title: The 2022 Energy Crisis: Topic Modelling and Sentiment Analysis of the Italian Twitter Discourse
abstract: Abstract Throughout 2022, the energy crisis has become a focal point in public discussions, receiving widespread attention within the media. Twitter has provided a significant avenue for individuals to participate in and shape the discourse by sharing messages with diverse types of content. This study explores a set of tweets to gain insights into how Italian-speaking users on the platform perceived and discussed the energy crisis and its associated facets. We primarily aim to uncover the most prominent topics, through the application of unsupervised topic modelling. Five main themes were identified: Energy Markets Dynamics, Ukraine Crisis, concerns over Energy Supply, Italian Politics, and Household Energy Consumption. By leveraging topic-tweet associations, we examined the prevalence of themes across the entire collection and analysed its evolution over time. In addition, a sentiment analysis was conducted on the same set of messages, following a dictionary-based approach. The distributions of sentiment scores across tweets revealed that the predominant topic of a tweet is associated with variations in sentiment, suggesting that certain themes evoke more strongly negative reactions than others. Finally, the economic analysis shows that Twitter sentiment co-moves with ISTAT consumer and business confidence indicators. The prevalence of discussions concerning household energy consumption and energy supplies also follows fluctuations in energy prices and consumption, suggesting that social-media discourse may provide timely signals of changing economic conditions during an energy crisis.

title: A comparison between ceiling-mounted FMCW, IR-UWB and Wi-Fi radar for in-bedroom human activity monitoring and sleep interruption detection
abstract: Despite their growing importance for contact-free radio frequency (RF) based healthcare monitoring, different radio technologies such as frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radar, impulse radio ultra-wideband (IR-UWB), and Wi-Fi sensing are rarely compared under identical deployment conditions, as existing studies typically differ in hardware, datasets, and evaluation methodologies. In addition, the performance of ceiling-mounted radars, despite their practical deployment and cost advantages in healthcare environments, remain underexplored. Therefore, this paper presents a controlled comparison and analysis of ceiling-mounted FMCW, IR-UWB, and Wi-Fi sensing using synchronized recordings from 20 participants across six room layouts. All technologies are evaluated with the same convolutional neural network (CNN) on both a fine-grained 10-class human activity recognition (HAR) task and a coarse 4-class sleep monitoring task. IR-UWB achieves the highest cross-subject activity recognition performance (89.0% macro F1), while FMCW generalizes best to unseen room layouts (83.8% macro F1). For sleep monitoring, all technologies exceed 92% macro F1 in unseen environments. The results reveal a fundamental trade-off between recognition performance and environmental robustness, which can be explained through differences in range resolution, antenna diversity, Doppler resolution, and spatial information retention. These findings provide practical guidelines for the design of healthcare-oriented RF sensing systems.

title: Architecture and Compilation Co-Design for High-Rate Quantum Product Codes on Neutral Atom Arrays
abstract: Achieving fault-tolerant quantum computing at a practical scale demands quantum error correction (QEC) codes with high encoding rates. Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes emerge as a promising candidate, especially given the rise of neutral atom arrays that provide dynamic long-range connectivity via atom movements. In general, synthesizing valid and efficient physical execution plans for QEC is a provably hard combinatorial problem, forming a critical compilation bottleneck that worsens as code sizes grow. To overcome this complexity, we focus on an important product family of qLDPC codes with dimension-reduction properties, and propose ONEX. This framework decomposes complex 2D physical execution planning into independent 1D subproblems, each solved to optimal execution depth within practical compilation time. First, we formulate the 1D execution plan with an explicit satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) encoding. This protocol produces provably depth-optimal solutions with substantial duration reduction. Second, we develop a multi-stage compilation pipeline featuring anytime optimization, movement compaction, and iterative feedback. This pipeline maintains practical wall-clock times while providing progressive refinement and on-demand retrieval of quality solutions. Third, we evaluate ONEX in the application of hypergraph product (HGP) code memory mapped onto neutral atom arrays, achieving 3.7x to 6.1x and 29.8x to 42.1x higher clock rates than the constructive 1D algorithm and the general 2D compiler, respectively, while scaling efficiently to codes with 2,500 data qubits. Finally, we extend ONEX to zoned layouts, revealing architectural insights into the associated trade-offs, and demonstrate its applicability to the broader lifted-product (LP) code family through a representative example.

title: Point-Based 3D Reconstruction from Sparse Views under Known Illumination
abstract: Sparse view 3D reconstruction is commonly addressed with neural implicit surfaces or dense point-based representations such as Gaussian splatting. Surface-aware splatting methods improve extracted geometry through oriented primitives and regularization, while RadiosityGS incorporates differentiable light transport through a radiosity inspired finite-element surfel formulation. We propose a differentiable point rendering method based on opacity-bearing beta surfels. An opacity explicit adjoint light transport formulation provides gradients for surfel geometry and appearance parameters, allowing physically based light transport to constrain reconstruction. Across five synthetic objects reconstructed from ten posed views, our method achieves the lowest mean symmetric Chamfer distance among the evaluated baselines and reduces mean Chamfer distance by 28.5% relative to the strongest point-based baseline while using only 267 surfels on average, approximately ~161 fewer primitives. Directional Chamfer results further show improved accuracy and competitive completion relative to related point-based methods. These results show that, in the controlled direct illumination setting, compact beta surfels combined with transport-based optimization can recover surfaces without relying on the tens to hundreds of thousands of primitives used by the evaluated baselines.

title: Proton emission half-lives and shape coexistence for 71 leq Z leq 83 odd-Z nuclei
abstract: One-proton emission is a direct probe of nuclear structure near the proton drip line and plays a critical role in understanding exotic decay modes and nucleosynthesis processes. In this study, we investigate the half-lives of one-proton emitters for 71 leq Z leq 83 odd-Z nuclei by employing the WKB approximation with nuclear potentials obtained from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum (DRHBc) and, for comparison, the relativistic continuum Hartree-Bogoliubov theory (RCHB). We first compare the calculated half-lives with available experimental data. The inclusion of quadrupole deformation via the DRHBc hardly contributes to improving the predictions of half-lives for the deformed nuclei. We find that all the studied nuclei exhibit ground states with |β_{2,{rm DRHBc}}| < 0.15, and within this limited deformation range the spectroscopic factor provides the dominant contribution to the half-life, compared to the decay width. In particular, for nuclei exhibiting shape coexistence in DRHBc, such as ^{170}Au, where the half-life varies significantly with the quadrupole deformation through its effect on the spectroscopic factor, we expect shape coexistence to exert a substantial influence on the variation of half-lives. Finally, we discuss the half-lives in consideration of shape coexistence. Our results indicate that the calculated half-life is governed not by the total-energy difference between coexisting minima but rather by the spectroscopic factor influenced by the deformation.

title: The Double-Edged Effect of Heightened Robot Attentiveness on Recommendation Acceptance
abstract: Robot attentiveness is typically viewed as a desirable service characteristic, yet its implications for robot recommendations are not straightforward. We conceptualize heightened robot attentiveness as a motive-ambiguous social cue: the same attentive behavior may signal genuine concern for customers while also suggesting an attempt to influence their choices. Adopting an attributional perspective, we integrate insights from social cognition and persuasion knowledge to explain these competing interpretations. We propose that greater robot attentiveness simultaneously increases perceived warmth and suspicion of ulterior motives, which exert opposing effects on consumers’ acceptance of robot recommendations. We further argue that customer–retailer relationship strength provides relational context for interpreting the motives underlying attentive robot behavior. Across two scenario-based experiments and a retrospective consumer survey, the findings consistently support this dual-path account. Greater robot attentiveness increases both perceived warmth and suspicion of ulterior motives, generating positive and negative indirect effects, respectively, on recommendation acceptance. Moreover, stronger customer–retailer relationships amplify the warmth pathway, whereas weaker relationships strengthen the suspicion pathway.

title: When the Vendor Changes the Firm: Vendor-Induced Routine Drift from Foundation Model Updates
abstract: Organizations increasingly embed externally supplied foundation models into recurring managerial decision processes. However, foundation-model providers can update underlying models while the adopting organization leaves its prompts, policies, workflows, decision criteria, employees, and business inputs unchanged. Such externally controlled updates may systematically alter AI-generated recommendations and, consequently, the enactment of organizational routines. This paper introduces Vendor-Induced Routine Drift (VIRD), defined as a systematic change in recurring organizational decision enactments attributable to a change in an externally controlled AI model while relevant organization-controlled conditions remain materially unchanged. Integrating organizational-routine theory, human–AI decision structures, resource dependence, and emerging research on foundation-model behavioral instability, the paper develops a theoretical framework explaining how vendor-side model updates may alter an organization’s effective decision policy without a conventional internally initiated change process. The paper distinguishes VIRD from ordinary model stochasticity, data drift, concept drift, deliberate digital transformation, model switching, and endogenous routine adaptation. It develops six propositions concerning model-version effects, decision ambiguity, AI autonomy, human review, policy codification, and organizational scale. A preregisterable empirical research design is proposed using approximately 2,000 standardized managerial decision scenarios across capital allocation, supplier selection, employee promotion, customer compensation, marketing allocation, and operational risk. The design holds organizational conditions constant while comparing documented foundation-model versions and explicitly separates cross-version effects from within-version stochastic variation. The central contribution is to theorize foundation-model version changes as potential organizational change events, rather than merely software maintenance or technical governance events. The paper argues that a third-party technology supplier may modify an embedded component of organizational judgment without the focal organization intentionally initiating organizational change. Keywords: Vendor-Induced Routine Drift; VIRD; Generative AI; Foundation Models; Organizational Routines; Organizational Change; Managerial Decision-Making; AI Governance; Human–AI Decision-Making; Strategic Management. Version: 1.0Publication type: Conceptual Working Paper / PreprintDate: August 20, 2026 This paper reports a theoretical framework and proposed empirical research protocol. It does not present fabricated, simulated-as-observed, or uncollected empirical results.

title: Uncovering Irregularities in National Identity Frameworks: An Algorithmic Approach to Anomaly Detection and LLM Based Predictive Auditing
abstract: Uncovering Irregularities in National Identity Frameworks: An Algorithmic Approach to Anomaly Detection and LLM Based Predictive Auditing 1Sounak Sarkar, 2Soumyashis Ghosh, 3Sourodeep Kar, 4Dr. Tirthadip Sinha 1,2UG student, Dept. of Computer Science & Engineering, Haldia Institute of Technology, Haldia, West Bengal 3UG student, Dept. of Electronics & Communication Engineering, Haldia Institute of Technology, Haldia, West Bengal 4Assistant Professor, Dept. of Electronics & Communication Engineering, Haldia Institute of Technology, Haldia, West Bengal ABSTRACT National biometric platforms like India's Aadhaar generate massive daily transaction volumes, making traditional reporting too slow to catch operational anomalies or sudden regional demand surges. To shift from reactive auditing to intelligent real-time monitoring, we introduce a predictive analytics engine using real-world UIDAI operational data (March–December 2025). Built on a decoupled React and FastAPI architecture, the platform features an automated time-series forecasting tournament. Using rolling-origin cross-validation with split-conformal prediction intervals, it delivers reliable capacity forecasts with precise statistical bounds. Concurrently, unsupervised Isolation Forests flag localized anomalies across state and district levels without requiring pre-labeled fraud data. A local LLM translates these technical insights into actionable, plain-language briefs backed by a human-in-the-loop audit trail—enabling swift, targeted field responses at national scale.

title: Security Architecture for AI Agent Systems
abstract: Large Language Model agents that call external tools are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection: adversarial instructions hidden in retrieved data can hijack the agent into unauthorised tool calls or data exfiltration. CaMeL (Google DeepMind, 2025), the foundational system-level defence, separates a Privileged LLM that never sees untrusted data from a Quarantined LLM that cannot call tools, and enforces capability-based taint tracking to reduce attack success to zero by design. But its guarantee assumes untrusted data never influences control flow — an assumption broken by common tasks such as triaging emails or routing queries, where which tool to call depends on data the planner has not yet seen. This thesis extends system-level defences to such data-dependent control flow and maps their limits. It reproduces CaMeL on AgentDojo with Claude Sonnet 4 (77.5% utility, 0% attack success across 560 attacks); presents a multi-label decomposition of 640 runs isolating data-dependent control flow as the largest irreducible architectural residue; and develops a four-category taxonomy (DDC-1 to DDC-4) with an explicit solvability boundary. It then proposes scope-guarded branching: the planner declares a fixed set of branches and per-branch tool scopes before any untrusted data is read, and a quarantined classifier selects among them without widening the action set. Across 240 adversarial runs, no tool call ever escaped the pre-declared scope, even at a 54–65% classifier-flip rate. The central principle is that security should rest not on the classifier's robustness, but on what the surrounding architecture statically constrains it to do.

title: Semantic Phase Space
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Semantic Phase Space (SPS), a novel framework that moves beyond traditional embedding techniques in natural language processing. SPS proposes that each semantic element – a word, a phrase, or even a complex concept – can be represented as a dynamic entity within a phase space, possessing attributes of position, velocity, and trajectory. This transforms language processing into Semantic Mechanics, treating language models as dynamical systems. The core of this approach lies in defining a mathematical space where semantic entities interact based on pre-defined rules and relationships, governed by equations that describe their evolution over time. This paper lays out the foundational principles of SPS, outlining the key elements of its construction and providing a theoretical basis for understanding language as a system of interacting dynamics. We explore the implications of this approach for various NLP tasks, focusing on the potential for enhanced understanding and generation through the application of dynamical systems theory. The central equation governing the evolution of a semantic element within its phase space is represented as: * *d/dt* (sᵢ) = f(sᵢ, sⱼ, t) Where *sᵢ* represents the state of the *i*-th semantic element, *sⱼ* represents the state of another semantic element, and *t* is time. The function *f* describes the interaction dynamics between the elements. This equation forms the basis for constructing the SPS and allows for the simulation of language processes. ---

title: Algorithm Crystallization
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to algorithm design termed "Algorithm Crystallization." Instead of traditional optimization methods which rely on iterative refinement of parameters, Algorithm Crystallization posits that algorithms evolve through a process analogous to crystal formation. The core concept involves allowing an algorithm to iteratively refine its internal representations and operations, driven by internal consistency checks and a tendency towards stability, leading to the formation of a "stable computational crystal." This crystal represents a highly refined and predictable algorithmic structure. The paper outlines the key principles of this methodology, focusing on the emergence of key characteristics within the crystal, including phase definitions, defect identification, and boundary stabilization. The theoretical framework presented suggests a fundamental shift in how we conceptualize and develop algorithms, moving away from explicit optimization toward a more emergent and self-organizing process. The core idea is that the algorithm "crystallizes" naturally through interaction and refinement, rather than being explicitly guided toward a solution through gradient descent or similar techniques. ---
