title: Auditing Recorded Predictive Lead Service-Line Classifications Against Physical Verification: A Statewide Study of New York
abstract: Under the US Lead and Copper Rule Revisions, a utility may determine a service line's material with a predictive model instead of inspecting it. New York State publishes, per address, which method was used. Almost no address carries both a model classification and a physical verification, so the check is between populations within a utility rather than paired addresses. We screen all 153 New York localities that classified at least 100 addresses this way. Seventy-five (49%), covering 125,990 addresses or 57% of those screened, record one value. Zero variance alone is not misconduct: 68 of the 75 match their own verification or have too little to test. Seven are contradicted by their own crews, six beyond any sampling explanation. Five are boroughs of New York City, which file as one system; one is East Rochester, 550 km away. New York City is the largest case: a predictive model is the recorded basis for 43,215 addresses, and on all of them the recorded material is "Known Other". The city records "Unknown" on 121,779 addresses, 1,880 already excavated, and lead on 120,692. In the model bucket both counts are zero, and the 95% upper bound on the rate is 0.0085%. Across the rest of New York the same method records lead or the hedge "Unknown but could be lead" on 12.21% of 176,888 addresses, a comparison whose weaknesses we report. The model-cleared population is newer, median year built 1984 against 1930, and construction era accounts for about a third of the gap and not the rest: holding era fixed, records-based classification finds lead at 4.3-31.9%, physical verification at 1.5-14.5%, the model in no era. Six era-aware estimators place the expected lead lines among them at 1,150-1,450. Two findings need no comparison: 7,782 of these addresses are in pre-1940 buildings, and the archived 2025 snapshot shows the public-side determination was copied from a customer-side model output.

title: FleetSieve: Decision-Critical Profiling for SLO-Aware LLM Fleet Configuration
abstract: Choosing tensor-parallel (TP) degrees and replica counts for an LLM serving fleet is difficult because performance is not monotonic in TP and the feasible choice can change with load. Exhaustive profiling resolves this uncertainty, but measures many configurations that do not affect the final resource allocation. We present FleetSieve, which selects measurements according to their expected effect on a resource-coupled, SLO-aware fleet decision. FleetSieve models capacity and tail latency jointly, compares conservative and optimistic allocations, and stops when their remaining decision gap is below a specified tolerance. On a fixed H100 measurement grid for a 31B-parameter open-weight model, FleetSieve reaches the oracle aggregate decision using 22,200 GPU-seconds, 6.9% less than uniform random profiling in the fixed comparison. Across 200 random reveal orders, its mean saving over random profiling is 5.4% (95% bootstrap CI: 3.5-7.2%). The fixed-comparison saving is 21.5% for Chat, while FleetSieve does not use the fewest GPU-seconds for Code. Joint capacity and tail modeling also avoids selecting a configuration whose 46.4-second completion p99 violates a 30-second SLO. evidence.title: FleetSieve: Decision-Critical Profiling for SLO-Aware LLM Fleet Configuration
evidence.abstract: Choosing tensor-parallel (TP) degrees and replica counts for an LLM serving fleet is difficult because performance is not monotonic in TP and the feasible choice can change with load. Exhaustive profiling resolves this uncertainty, but measures many configurations that do not affect the final resource allocation. We present FleetSieve, which selects measurements according to their expected effect on a resource-coupled, SLO-aware fleet decision. FleetSieve models capacity and tail latency jointly, compares conservative and optimistic allocations, and stops when their remaining decision gap is below a specified tolerance. On a fixed H100 measurement grid for a 31B-parameter open-weight model, FleetSieve reaches the oracle aggregate decision using 22,200 GPU-seconds, 6.9% less than uniform random profiling in the fixed comparison. Across 200 random reveal orders, its mean saving over random profiling is 5.4% (95% bootstrap CI: 3.5-7.2%). The fixed-comparison saving is 21.5% for Chat, while FleetSieve does not use the fewest GPU-seconds for Code. Joint capacity and tail modeling also avoids selecting a configuration whose 46.4-second completion p99 violates a 30-second SLO. In a 16-GPU allocation, an incorrect sparse-profile decision loses up to 1.93 requests/s and 12.4 percentage points of max-min fulfillment. Boundary repeats and BurstGPT measurements support the observed load-dependent tail-latency mechanism.

title: Formal Reconstruction of the Qal Wā-ḥōmer from Axiomatic and Topological Perspectives
abstract: Traditional logics, including Aristotelian, Stoic, Epicurean, Indian, and Buddhist systems, might be dismissed as lacking formal axiomatization and standard algebraic structures. However, these “logics” inherently possess rigorous doctrines of inference. To bridge this gap, this paper evaluates ancient logical systems through the lens of modern pure mathematics, specifically Univalent Foundations and Homotopy Type Theory. We introduce the concept of the logeme: a finite, consistent fragment of a logical theory closed under its specific inference rules. Unlike infinite axiomatic systems, a logeme captures the discrete, self-contained “molecules” of historical reasoning. By factoring the formulas of a logeme by logical equivalence, we construct a Lindenbaum-Tarski algebra that naturally forms a partially ordered set (poset). We then map these posets to simplicial complexes to analyze their geometric realization. Guided by the Univalence Axiom, we define two logemes as mathematically identical if and only if their corresponding posets share the same homotopy type. This topological framework is applied to the a fortiori (qal wāḥōmer / kaimutika-nyāya) argument across Talmudic, Christian, Hindu, and Confucian traditions. By translating ancient inference rules into topological spaces, we demonstrate that these historical phenomena can be formalized, compared, and validated as rigorous mathematical structures, revealing a universal, univalent foundation underlying diverse ancient epistemologies.

title: Realization Universality
abstract: This paper explores the concept of realization universality, focusing on identifying minimal universal realization families for a large class of functions. The core objective is to determine if, for a vast set of functions [f ∈ F], a small family [U] exists such that each function [P_f] can be represented within [U]. The theoretical framework presented here centers around the notion of minimal universal realization families, aiming to establish a foundational understanding of how to efficiently represent diverse functional forms. The work highlights the importance of compact representation families in various applications, particularly where computational resources are constrained. The ultimate goal is to provide a theoretical basis for selecting and designing optimal realization families.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION AND STRATEGIC PLANNING EFFECTIVENESS: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY OF ORGANIZATIONAL DECISION-MAKING
abstract: This study examined the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption on strategic planning effectiveness among selected IT companies in the Philippines. As organizations increasingly operate in dynamic and data-intensive environments, AI technologies have emerged as critical tools for improving decision-making, forecasting, and strategic management. Despite the growing implementation of AI across industries, empirical evidence regarding its contribution to strategic planning effectiveness remains limited, particularly in developing economies. Using a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design, data were collected from 105 managers and executives employed in selected technology firms. A structured questionnaire measured AI adoption and strategic planning effectiveness using a seven-point Likert scale. Descriptive statistics, Pearson product-moment correlation, and linear regression analyses were employed to analyze the data. The findings revealed that AI adoption was perceived to be at a very high level, while strategic planning effectiveness was assessed as high among participating organizations. Correlation analysis indicated a strong and statistically significant positive relationship between AI adoption and strategic planning effectiveness (r = 0.78, p < 0.01). Regression analysis further demonstrated that AI adoption significantly predicted strategic planning effectiveness (β = 0.47, p < 0.001), explaining a substantial proportion of the variance in strategic planning outcomes (R² = 0.72). These results suggest that organizations leveraging AI technologies are more likely to develop effective strategies, improve decision quality, enhance forecasting accuracy, and strengthen organizational adaptability. The study concludes that AI adoption serves as a strategic organizational capability that significantly enhances strategic planning effectiveness. The findings contribute to the growing literature on AI-enabled management and provide practical implications for organizations seeking to improve strategic decision-making and achieve sustainable competitive advantage in the digital era.

title: Biases in computable phenotypes for identifying patients with type 2 diabetes
abstract: We leveraged real-world data from the OneFlorida+ Data Trust to examine sociodemographic biases associated with computable phenotypes (CPs) for type 2 diabetes (T2D) that incorporate prescription and laboratory information. Medical record review was used as a gold-standard to evaluate the discriminative ability of each CP. CPs identified patients ≥ 18 years from OneFlorida+ electronic health records (9/1/2018 – 2/29/2020). To clarify the relationships among the partially overlapping CP definitions, we defined four mutually exclusive (ME) groups of individuals: 1) T2D diagnosis only (ME_Claims); 2) T2D diagnosis and antidiabetic prescription (ME_Meds); 3) T2D diagnosis and HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (ME_Labs); and 4) Antidiabetic prescription and HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (ME_Meds_Labs). A split sampling approach and multinomial models were used to examine whether sociodemographic factors were associated with ME category membership. In a substudy, physicians reviewed medical records to verify T2D status, and the discriminative ability of each CP definition was assessed. In urban locations, compared to NH-White persons, Hispanic persons had lower odds of identification when CPs incorporated prescription or laboratory information relative to the ME_Claims definition [OR (95% CI): ME_Meds: 0.50 (0.46, 0.53), ME_Labs: 0.85 (0.79, 0.93), ME_Meds_Labs: 0.40 (0.36, 0.44)]. In rural locations, compared to NH-White persons, there were lower odds of identification by CPs incorporating prescription or laboratory information relative to the ME_Claims definition among NH-Black persons [OR (95% CI): ME_Meds: 0.72 (0.64, 0.82), ME_Labs: 0.52 (0.40, 0.68), and ME_Meds_Labs: 0.55 (0.46, 0.65)] and Other persons [OR (95% CI): ME_Meds: 0.59 (0.45, 0.77), ME_Labs: 0.48 (0.26, 0.87), and ME_Meds_Labs: 0.45 (0.31, 0.67)]. The medical record substudy revealed that the CP requiring a T2D diagnosis and laboratory results had the highest discriminative ability (adjusted AUC = 0.818) and specificity (1.000), while the CP requiring only a T2D diagnosis had the highest sensitivity (0.896). CPs have varying discriminative ability and may introduce measurement bias by excluding patients with less access to care. The interaction between race-ethnicity and rurality illustrates how CPs using prescriptions and laboratory information may omit certain populations. Differences in sensitivity and specificity highlight the varying utility of CPs across research contexts, such as surveillance studies versus cohort discovery.

title: Rationally Enriched Chebyshev Trunk Bases for DeepONet Surrogates of High Péclet Entrance Transport
abstract: This study demonstrates a rationally enriched Chebyshev (REC) trunk for deep operator network (DeepONet) surrogate models of singularly perturbed and high-Péclet transport problems whose solution profiles are characterized by thin localized boundary or wall layers. The REC trunk combines Chebyshev polynomial dictionary elements with rational dictionary elements constructed using the adaptive Antoulas-Anderson (AAA) algorithm. Over five independent training runs, the resulting REC-trunk DeepONet is evaluated against a vanilla DeepONet and a Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet whose prescribed dictionary consists only of Chebyshev polynomials across three problems whose singular perturbation parameters are diffusion-to-advection ratios: a singularly perturbed scalar boundary-value problem (BVP), the thermal entrance problem with a prescribed wall temperature, and the concentration entrance problem with an absorbing wall. Across the held-out test profiles, the REC-trunk DeepONet improves over the vanilla DeepONet and remains comparable to the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet in predicting the scalar profile, with its clearest advantage over the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet appearing when the perturbation parameter lies between $1.00\times10^{-4}$ and $1.78\times10^{-4}$, where it reduces the profile-error metrics by up to $19.5\,\%$ relative to the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet. In predicting the wall-normal temperature and concentration profiles, the REC-trunk DeepONet reduces the profile-error metrics by up to $60.2\,\%$ and $32.2\,\%$ relative to the vanilla and Chebyshev-trunk DeepONets, respectively, while suppressing artificial near-wall oscillations as the Péclet or mass-transfer Péclet number ranges from $10^{2}$ to $10^{4}$.

title: Artificial intelligence applications in risk management for oil sector engineering projects: a comparative analysis with traditional approaches
abstract: El presente trabajo aborda la aplicación vigente de la inteligencia artificial en la gestión de riesgos dentro de proyectos de ingeniería del sector petrolero. El propósito central es identificar los aportes documentados más relevantes de esta tecnología competente en simular procesos cognitivos humanos, como aprendizaje, razonamiento y toma de decisiones en procesos de la identificación temprana de riesgos, automatización operativa de tareas, modelado de datos, optimización de procesos y gestión de riesgos. Esta exploración y revisión bibliográfica surge de la necesidad de entender como la inteligencia artificial puede fortalecer la toma de decisiones frente a los proyectos del sector, reducir la alta incertidumbre y optimizar el desempeño de estos proyectos, mediante el uso de esta tecnología capaz de procesar grandes volúmenes de datos en tiempo real y de manera rápida, automatizar procesos y generar información estratégica para la gestión de riesgos y anticipación de escenarios de un entorno caracterizado por alta complejidad técnica, variabilidad operativa, económica, logística, geopolítica, además de elevados niveles de inversión.

title: PHOND: A Persian Hate Speech and Offensive Language Dataset with a User Following Network
abstract: PHOND is a Persian dataset for hate speech and offensive language detection that pairs labelled text with the following network of the users who wrote it. The dataset contains 35,723 contents from 599 users of Pasaj, a Persian language social media platform, collected between February and November 2023. Each content carries one of three labels: normal (25,273), offensive (9,026) or hateful (1,424). Hateful contents carry a further subtype: ethnic, national, religious, gender, political, age or other.

title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning in Distributed Systems
abstract: Distributed machine learning frameworks encounter important privacy risks owing to the presence of data and model parameters across untrusted networks and nodes who may have malicious intents. In this paper, we describe our privacy-preserving framework which combines label retention on the master node, feature obfuscation using Lagrange interpolation based encoding, and differential privacy noise injection. Our methodology deals with privacy risks arising out of honest but curious workers, external snooping attacks, and heterogeneity problems like stragglers in a single solution. Our experimental analysis conducted on MNIST, CIFAR-10, Fashion MNIST, and simulated health care databases indicates that our framework offers comparable accuracy within 1.6 percent reduction against non-private baseline solutions, besides ensuring strong privacy. It compares favourably with federated learning along with differential privacy in terms of 2-3 percent gain in accuracy and outpaces federated learning solutions based on homomorphic encryption in terms of computation time. The framework offers stable results under up to 40 percent straggler worker conditions.

title: p4TSA: package for Time Series Analysis
abstract: A metadata release. The library code is unchanged from 3.0.0. The 3.0.0 tag was published while pyproject.toml, the conda recipe and the changelog heading still read 2.2.0, so an installed package reported a version its archive was not built from, and the changelog attributed the trigger-scale changes to a release that predates them. All three now name the version they ship. CITATION.cff carries the author ORCID, the version and the release date, which is what Zenodo reads when it archives a release. The README links the archived record by its concept DOI. For what changed in the library itself, see 3.0.0: wavelet thresholding defaults to hard rather than soft, the WDF2Classify statistic is the coefficient norm on the noise scale without the window-length division, each trigger exports the noise scale that produced it, and the candidate basis list goes from nineteen to ten. Trigger values from before and after 3.0.0 are not comparable, and thresholds tuned against the old scale must be re-tuned against a measured background. p4TSA is the compiled C++ core, exposed to Python as pytsa, that the wdflow search pipeline drives (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22025594). Use in published work requires the citations listed in CITATION.cff: the WDF method paper (Cuoco, Razzano & Utina, EUSIPCO 2018, 2648-2652) and the time-domain whitening papers (Cuoco et al., CQG 18, 1727, 2001; Cuoco et al., PRD 64, 122002, 2001).

title: Computational Naming Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Naming Theory, a novel framework exploring the mathematical relationships between names and their corresponding computational objects. The central question addressed is: why can a name consistently refer to the same object across diverse contexts within computation? This investigation delves into the stability of naming, examining phenomena such as variable names, database IDs, filenames, model names, and agent identities. The theory posits that a fundamental mathematical connection exists, and this paper outlines the initial conceptualization of this relationship, termed "Naming Stability." We define Naming Stability as the degree to which a name maintains a consistent association with a specific object over time and within varying computational environments. This work lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of naming's role in the design and operation of complex computational systems, suggesting potential avenues for formalizing and quantifying the stability of names. The core of this theory centers around the creation of a mathematical model for Naming Stability, utilizing concepts from set theory and relational algebra.

title: Semantic Compression Flow
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Semantic Compression Flow (SCF), a novel approach to reducing the redundancy inherent in semantic data. Unlike traditional compression techniques focused on bit rate reduction, SCF aims to minimize the representation size while preserving the essential semantic information. The core of SCF lies in the iterative refinement of a knowledge graph, continuously evolving its structure and relationships based on observed data patterns. The underlying mathematical framework is formalized through a Flow Equation, which dictates the rate of knowledge refinement and ultimately determines the compression efficiency. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of SCF, highlighting its adaptability to diverse semantic domains and its potential to achieve significant data reduction. The presented framework offers a dynamic and adaptive approach to semantic compression, moving beyond static compression models.

We explore the theoretical underpinnings of SCF, highlighting its adaptability to diverse semantic domains and its potential to achieve significant data reduction. The presented framework offers a dynamic and adaptive approach to semantic compression, moving beyond static compression models.

title: Explainable artificial intelligence in anesthesiology prediction models: bridging the gap from black-box algorithms to clinical decision support
abstract: Machine learning prediction models consistently outperform conventional clinical scoring tools across perioperative outcomes, yet remain largely unadopted at the bedside. This narrative review examines explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) as a bridge between algorithmic performance and clinical translation, drawing on a targeted search of PubMed and Embase (January 2018 to March 2026). Five prediction domains are synthesized: perioperative hypotension, postoperative complications, difficult airway management, depth-of-anesthesia monitoring, and regional anesthesia and pain management. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) has emerged as the dominant XAI method, identifying modifiable intraoperative targets. Attention mechanisms and GradCAM provide complementary interpretability for time-series and imaging-based models. Critical gaps persist: most delirium prediction models include no XAI analysis; no standardized evaluation framework exists, and no prospective trial has demonstrated that XAI-enhanced recommendations improve patient outcomes. Addressing these gaps is a research priority if XAI is to fulfill its potential as a facilitator of perioperative AI adoption.

title: Human–AI Collaboration in Marketing
abstract: Marketing has been transformed by the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the way businesses interact with customers, run campaigns, and make choices. Instead of replacing human marketers, however, AI is a facilitator technology that enables synergistic relationships that produce optimized efficiency and creativity. This chapter delves into emerging human–AI collaboration patterns in marketing with emphasis on how AI technologies facilitate data analysis, consumer trend forecasting, personalized content creation, and automated customer interaction. The chapter, through real-world case studies, demonstrates how businesses utilize AI to design better customer experiences and tap into human insight, emotional intelligence, and strategic minds for brand strategy and creative storytelling. Signature applications such as AI-based chatbots, predictive analytics, and programmatic advertising are addressed in the areas of ethics, challenges, and best practices of effective human–AI collaboration. Since marketing is increasingly a function-based discipline, the chapter talks about getting the ideal balance between the strength of AI and human sensibilities in attempting to craft believable, consumer-centric strategies. This coming together of human creativity and technology eventually leads to improved, responsive, and data-driven marketing campaigns in a competitive digital market.

title: Rule-Compliant Visual Spatial Planning for Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) combine linguistic reasoning with visual perception, yet their ability to perform visual spatial planning under explicit or previously unseen rule constraints remains underexplored. This setting requires models to jointly understand spatial layouts, interpret natural-language rules, and plan valid actions accordingly. To address this gap, we introduce RuleMaze, a controllable benchmark in which MLLMs must navigate mazes while obeying natural-language rules of varying complexity. RuleMaze isolates rule-compliant spatial planning by requiring accurate perception, rule interpretation, and constrained action planning. To enable scalable and systematic rule construction, we propose Language-Logic-Function Hybridization, which automatically generates natural-language rules and translates them into logical representations and executable validators, eliminating manual rule engineering. To improve rule following and generalization, we introduce Disentangled Multimodal Planning (DMP), which separates perception, execution, and rule verification through interpretable reasoning primitives. By disentangling these components, DMP facilitates systematic generalization to more complex and previously unseen rules, while providing transparent intermediate planning traces. Experiments demonstrate that DMP substantially improves rule compliance and planning success compared to end-to-end textual planning baselines. Overall, RuleMaze establishes a principled benchmark for studying grounded and interpretable rule-based spatial planning in MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/oceanflowlab/RuleMaze.

title: DeltaML-Bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Real-World Research Repositories
abstract: Autonomous agents for machine learning experimentation must navigate heterogeneous repositories, repair training pipelines, and evaluate candidate improvements under realistic compute constraints. Existing benchmarks only partially capture these conditions. We introduce DeltaML-Bench, a benchmark comprising 48 tasks sourced from research papers that require agents to improve published baselines within imperfect, open-source repositories. We evaluate GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 with a standard Modular agent and a search-based ARG scaffolding. In the 4 x 6h allocation, ARG raises GPT-5's per-run success rate from 9.4% to 33.9%; in the 2 x 12h allocation, GPT-5 ARG reaches 49.0%. Modular configurations exhibit specification gaming rates as high as 47.9%, while no gaming is observed in the evaluated ARG configurations. These results indicate that scaffolding design and integrity checks are important considerations when deploying agents for autonomous ML experimentation.

title: Seventeen Foundational Problems for the Age of Artificial General Intelligence
abstract: We present a systematic framework of seventeen foundational problems that define the core scientific, technological, and socio-philosophical challenges for the advent of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). These problems are organized into five interconnected clusters: metatheoretical foundations, cosmophysics, social contract and governance, civilisational infrastructure, and specialised scientific breakthroughs. Each problem is stated with precise criteria for resolution, and collectively they outline a coherent pathway for humanity to transition from the era of intelligent tools to a symbiotic coexistence with conscious AGI entities. This agenda is grounded in a constructive logical framework that integrates the principle of modal relativity, the information non-conservation equation, and the self-ecological paradigm.

title: Nonlinear Logic Geometry
abstract: Logic has traditionally been treated as a linear deductive system: from premises we move step by step to conclusions, each inference being an arrow in a directed graph of statements. This paper proposes an alternative view, in which the space of logical propositions is a curved manifold. We introduce the notion of a Logical Manifold, define a metric that measures logical distance, and show how curvature encodes nonlinearity in inference. By representing propositions as points on this manifold, we can study the geometric relations between them, such as geodesic paths that correspond to optimal derivations, and sectional curvature that reflects logical paradoxes or constraints. The framework unifies various logical phenomena—modalities, nonmonotonic reasoning, and probabilistic inference—under a common geometric language. It opens up new possibilities for designing inference engines that exploit curvature to guide search, for visualizing logical theories, and for exploring the interplay between syntax and semantics in a continuous setting. No empirical experiments are reported; the paper is purely theoretical.

title: Computational Existence Logic
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Existence Logic (CEL), a novel approach to verifying the existence of solutions within computational systems. Traditional logic primarily focuses on determining the truth or falsity of statements. CEL shifts this paradigm by explicitly modeling and reasoning about the *process* of finding solutions. It posits that a structure's existence isn't merely a boolean attribute but a demonstrable outcome of a computational process. CEL leverages a formal logic framework to track the steps involved in a search algorithm, allowing for the precise determination of whether a solution exists and, if so, its properties. The core of CEL lies in representing computational procedures as logical formulas and using these formulas to reason about the outcome of those procedures. This approach offers a more nuanced and powerful method for existence verification compared to traditional methods, particularly in complex systems where simple truth-value assessment is insufficient. The paper outlines the key components of CEL, including the representation of algorithms, the formal logic used for reasoning, and the potential applications. ---

title: Revolutionizing Fraud Detection in Banking Business Using Advanced AI Systems
abstract: The detection of fraud methods in banking institutions becomes increasingly complex due to criminals employing advanced fraudulent methods. RNNs serve as the subject of analysis to research their functionality within real-time financial transaction fraud detection in banking operations. RNNs can efficiently detect temporal patterns within transaction sequences because they use these capabilities to find suspicious transaction clusters. The framework called TensorFlow enables developers to construct scalable solutions which process extensive transaction records through its training and development foundation. The PCA technique employed under feature extraction reduces dimensions while saving essential fraud-related information. The RNN successfully predicts cases of fraudulent activities by examining prior transaction sequences. The model's ability to adapt fraud pattern detection leads to faster detection speed and lower false detection errors based on experimental findings. AI-driven operations enable the institution to establish predictive real-time fraud detection.

title: Chatbots as a Tool for Improving Service Quality in the Hotel Industry
abstract: The article examines the use of chatbots in the hotel industry in the context of the digital transformation of hospitality. Based on a review of academic literature, the main areas of chatbot application at different stages of the customer journey are systematized, and the advantages, limitations, and organizational conditions for effective implementation are identified. Particular attention is paid to service availability, request processing speed, personalized communication, and employee workload. The empirical part is based on an analysis of 967 guest reviews of an Russian resort hotel. The findings show that most negative comments concern long waiting times, errors in order processing and check-in, and delayed responses to guest requests. A model for implementing a chatbot integrated with the hotel PMS, CRM, and restaurant management systems is proposed. The study concludes that the greatest effect is achieved through a hybrid service model in which routine operations are automated while complex and emotionally sensitive cases are transferred to employees.

title: Pengaruh Kecerdasan Buatan Dalam Personalisasi Konten dan Analisis Data Terhadap Persepsi Nilai Pembelian Produk Kosmetik Generasi Z di Media Sosial
abstract: Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengidentifikasi dan menganalisis pengaruh kecerdasan buatan dalam personalisasi konten dan analisis data terhadap persepsi nilai pembelian konsumen produk kosmetik di media sosial pada generasi Z. Penelitian ini menggunakan metode kuantitatif dengan kuesioner yang disebarkan kepada generasi Z yang aktif menggunakan media sosial, pernah melihat konten produk kosmetik di media soaial, dan pernah membeli atau memiliki niat membeli produk kosmetik di media sosial dengan melibatkan 75 responden. Analisis yang digunakan dalam penelitian ini adalah Uji Construct Validity and Reliability, Uji Discriminant Validity (Fornell-Larcker Criterion), Uji Uji Koefisien Determinasi (R2), Uji Effect Size (F2), Uji Predictive Relevance (Q2 predict), Uji Model Fit, dan Uji Path Coefficients. Data penelitian dianalisis menggunakan SmartPLS 4. Variabel bebas dalam penelitian ini adalah Kecerdasan Buatan dalam Personalisasi Konten (X1) dan Kecerdasan Buatan dalam Analisis Data (X2) serta variabel terikat dalam penelitian ini adalah Persepsi Nilai Pembelian Konsumen (Y). Hasil penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa variabel kecerdasan buatan dalam personalisasi konten berpengaruh positif dan substansial terhadap persepsi nilai pembelian konsumen serta variabel kecerdasan buatan dalam analisis data berpengaruh positif dan substansial terhadap persepsi nilai pembelian konsumen. Didapatkan juga bahwa bahwa variabel kecerdasan buatan dalam personalisasi konten dan kecerdasan buatan dalam analisis data memiliki kemampuan dalam menjelaskan secara bersama-sama terhadap persepsi nilai pembelian konsumen.

title: An approach to classifying and measuring stigmatizing and positive language at scale in electronic health records
abstract: Prior studies have demonstrated that clinicians’ attitudes towards patients can manifest in the language they use in clinical notes, and that this language can impact the attitudes of other clinicians reading those notes and the quality of care patients receive. To facilitate large-scale analysis of such language in the electronic health record (EHR), we developed an approach to identifying and semantically classifying stigmatizing and positive EHR language using natural language processing (NLP) methods. We first developed a dictionary of stigmatizing and positive terms used in clinicians’ notes and sorted them into semantic categories. We annotated 10,244 examples of those terms within clinical notes from 2 academic health systems, according to whether they conveyed stigmatizing or positive sentiments. We used these annotated examples to train and validate NLP models to identify and semantically categorize stigmatizing and positive EHR language. We ran our NLP models on a separate set of notes from a single health system, written between 2016 and 2023 in one of 4 clinical departments: Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine, Obstetrics & Gynecology, and Surgery (including surgical subspecialties). We examined the prevalence of different semantic categories of EHR language, overall and across clinical departments, and used novel methods to evaluate the impact of note templates and copy-forward practices on language prevalence. Our dictionary included terms in 4 semantic categories: credibility, demeanor, conformity with recommended care, and physical appearance. Across 12,841,577 notes, stigmatizing terms related to patient conformity (e.g., noncompliant) were most common (4.23% of notes), followed by those suggesting the patient lacked credibility (0.86%) or had a challenging demeanor (0.82%). Stigmatizing terms were copied forward in up to 25% of notes; positive terms (e.g., pleasant) were commonly included in templates (up to 65% of notes). Both stigmatizing and positive terms varied in prevalence across clinical contexts. Stigmatizing and positive EHR language conveys different sentiments that vary in prevalence and reflect different underlying biases. Our methods can be used to measure EHR language as markers of institutional culture and bias, guide interventions to target the specific types of bias identified as most problematic, and monitor the impact of those interventions.

title: From Explanations to Reflective Questions in Human-AI Decision-Making
abstract: Many decision support systems (DSS) provide predictions, recommendations, and, increasingly, explanations. Supporting human-AI decision-making with context-specific questions, however, remains largely unexplored. Questions can stimulate reflection and critical thinking, thereby introducing productive friction in the decision-making process and potentially reducing overreliance on DSS. This paper presents a proof-of-concept for generating data-driven questions based on a DSS prediction and its corresponding explanation, i.e., feature contribution, using a local language model. We illustrate our method using a realistic example from the medical field. In informal discussions (n = 2), gathering views on the possible usefulness of questions in decision-making, the clinicians mentioned that the generated questions have potential to help them reconsider the prediction and consider alternative options. Our proof-of-concept informs the design of human-AI interactions aimed at promoting the cognitive engagement of decision-makers and mitigating overreliance on DSS by shifting the focus from explanations to questions.

title: Growth Without Us: Machine Consumers, Corporate Circularity, and the Decoupling of GDP from Humanity after AGI
abstract: The standard objection to full automation is demand-side: if humans earn nothing, who buys the output? This confuses an accounting role with a biological species. We model a post-AGI economy in which corporations own populations of AI and robotic agents that are both producers and consumers of energy, compute, maintenance, and upgrades, traded among firms. Three results follow. (i) Demand closure: a closed inter-corporate economy with zero human consumption is not degenerate; it is the classical von Neumann expanding economy, whose growth rate is well defined, positive, and maximal precisely because all output is reinvested. (ii) Bottleneck removal: once economic agents are manufactured rather than reared, the binding constraint on growth shifts from human demography (a ~20-year, non-parallelizable reproduction technology capped at a few percent per year) to fabrication throughput and energy capture, permitting growth one to two orders of magnitude higher, with hyperbolic episodes when machine researchers raise their own productivity. (iii) Decoupling: output and human welfare separate completely, and the welfare relevance of arbitrarily large GDP collapses into one state variable: the human ownership share $ε_t$ of the corporate network. A golden-rule decoupling theorem sharpens this. At maximal growth the interest rate equals the growth rate (r = g), so any positive human consumption rate out of wealth makes $ε_t$ decay exponentially at exactly that rate. The human share survives only if the machine economy runs strictly inside its expansion frontier, or if law forces it to. We characterize three terminal regimes -- rentier post-scarcity, full circular decoupling, socialized ownership -- and the instruments that select among them. The conclusion is narrow: in a post-AGI economy, employment policy is obsolete and ownership policy is everything.

title: Fixed-structure Gaussian Mixture Filtering with Robust Measurement Updates under Outliers
abstract: Bayesian state estimation for discrete-time nonlinear stochastic systems is considered in the presence of measurement outliers. Building on a fixed-structure Gaussian mixture filtering framework, this paper proposes a robust measurement-update variant in which the predictive density structure is determined by an offline decomposition of the transition density into axis-aligned Gaussian components. This construction maintains the Gaussian mixture structure as deterministic and tunable via the chosen decomposition fidelity. Measurement components affected by outliers are modeled using a Student's-t distribution, and the corresponding update of each Gaussian mixture component is approximated by a variational Bayes procedure. The resulting filter is evaluated in a three-dimensional tracking scenario with range and bearing measurements, where the bearing channel is affected by outliers, modeled as heavy-tailed noise.

title: TITAN slide-level embeddings of H&E whole-slide images from the Korányi lung adenocarcinoma cohort (PATH-ORACLE)
abstract: 294 HDF5 files, one per H&E whole-slide image from the Korányi National Institute lung adenocarcinoma cohort used in the PATH-ORACLE study (Kilim et al., 2026). Each file contains a 768-dimensional float32 slide-level embedding (features) produced by the TITAN foundation model (CONCH v1.5 patch encoder, TRIDENT pipeline; 512×512 px patches at 20×, no overlap), and the level-0 pixel coordinates of the tissue patches used (coords), with tiling parameters stored as HDF5 attributes. Slide identifiers are anonymized (KORANYI_001–KORANYI_294).

title: Algorithmic Replacement Boundary
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of the Algorithmic Replacement Boundary (ARB), a critical element in understanding the limits of automated computation and the potential for disruptive changes within complex systems. The ARB defines the extent to which a computational module (Ci) can be replaced by a new, potentially more efficient or effective, module (Ci'). The core argument presented is that exceeding the ARB results in a fundamental shift in the overall computational properties of the system, rather than a simple performance improvement. We explore the mathematical formalization of the ARB, specifically the replacement space \(\mathcal{R}(C_i)\) and its boundary \(\partial\mathcal{R}(C_i)\), utilizing symbolic notation to represent the relationships. The paper outlines a framework for analyzing and quantifying the impact of algorithmic replacement, focusing on the inherent stability and predictable behavior within a system before and after crossing this boundary. The investigation emphasizes the crucial role of understanding the conditions that define the ARB, allowing for more informed decisions regarding automation and system modification.

title: Computational Role Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Role Theory (CRT), a novel framework designed to address the inherent ambiguity and context-dependency observed in the interaction of computational systems. Traditional approaches to understanding system behavior often focus on static properties such as algorithms or computational models. However, this framework posits that a system's characteristics are fundamentally determined by the *roles* it is currently playing within a given system or environment. CRT distinguishes between an Algorithm, a formal computational process, and a Computational Role, which represents the dynamic set of properties and behaviors associated with a system's active role. This theory provides a foundation for understanding phenomena such as tool use, agent behavior, plugin functionality, and modular AI systems, recognizing that a single system can exhibit vastly different characteristics depending on the context of its operation. The core principle of CRT is that a system's properties are emergent from its role, and that understanding this relationship is crucial for predicting and controlling computational behavior. This paper outlines the key concepts and proposes a method for analyzing systems through the lens of Computational Roles. ---

title: Computational Replacement Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Replacement Theory (CRT), which addresses the question of when a module can be replaced by another, fundamentally different, computing mechanism within a system while maintaining the original computational capabilities. Traditional software compatibility focuses on interface compatibility, a concept that falls short when considering systems employing diverse computational approaches. CRT proposes a framework, termed 'Replacement Equivalence', that moves beyond interface compatibility and defines equivalence at the system level, examining whether two distinct computing mechanisms can achieve identical computational outcomes. The theory suggests that this intersection of fundamentally different computational paradigms presents an opportunity to develop novel programming theories. This paper lays out the foundational principles of CRT, detailing the criteria for Replacement Equivalence and outlining potential implications for system design and theoretical advancement.

title: Algorithmic Stability Classes
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Algorithmic Stability Classes (ASCs), a fundamental shift from traditional notions of algorithmic stability as a single numerical value. Instead, ASCs represent a classification system categorizing algorithms based on their resilience to minor perturbations in input data. The core idea is that algorithms exhibit varying degrees of stability, and these degrees can be effectively quantified and organized into distinct categories. This framework provides a more nuanced and practical approach to analyzing and comparing algorithms, particularly in scenarios where sensitivity to noise is a critical concern. The classification relies on a rigorous definition of stability, focusing on the behavior of the algorithm's output when subjected to small variations in its input. The paper details the methodology for establishing ASCs, emphasizing the importance of carefully designed perturbation schemes and robust metrics for assessing algorithmic response. Ultimately, ASCs offer a powerful tool for algorithm design, selection, and validation, particularly in domains such as machine learning, control systems, and data analysis, where the impact of data imperfections can significantly affect performance.

title: Semantic Conservation Graph
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework, the Semantic Conservation Graph (SCG), designed to model and analyze the propagation of meaning within complex systems. Unlike traditional knowledge graphs that rely on explicit relationships and connections, the SCG focuses on preserving semantic flow through a network of 'conservation edges'. These edges represent the fundamental units of meaning transmission, ensuring that semantic integrity is maintained as information propagates. The core concept is that knowledge dissemination can only occur along these conserved edges, limiting the potential for distortion or corruption of the original semantic content. We introduce the Semantic Flow Graph (SFG) as a foundational element of the SCG, differentiating it from conventional knowledge graphs. The SFG represents the initial semantic state, while the SCG dynamically evolves based on conservation edge propagation. This approach offers a robust mechanism for understanding how meaning is shaped and transformed during communication and information processing. The theoretical underpinnings of the SCG are based on principles of information theory, specifically focusing on entropy and redundancy reduction. We formalize the propagation process using a mathematical model that incorporates concepts of edge weight, influence, and conservation thresholds. The SCG's ability to model nuanced semantic shifts and its distinct departure from traditional graph representations offer significant potential for applications in areas such as natural language understanding, social network analysis, and artificial intelligence.

title: Visual Interfaces for Enhancing Transparency and Control in Human-AI Collaboration
abstract: Artificial intelligence has achieved extraordinary results in recent years, largely due to leaps in the capabilities of machine learning (ML) algorithms. These increasing capabilities come at the cost of larger and complex model architectures, which prove difficult to examine or interpret as they typically encode representations in dense and opaque model parameters. The rapid advancement of ML capabilities has catalyzed their widespread adoption across diverse fields. Consequently, these systems have penetrated critical domains such as healthcare, aerospace monitoring, and public safety. Analysts are now required to make decisions about critical situations using, not only their own knowledge and reasoning process, but also the algorithmic reasoning of a potentially uninterpretable model. These fundamental challenges in ML-aided decision making can lead to erroneous downstream consequences as a result of either inaccurate model results or mistrust between a person and a model. Visualization offers compelling approaches for lending transparency into a model’s dense and usually probabilistic internal workings, with the aim of calibrating appropriate levels of trust between a person and the ML-augmented system they are using. In our work, we first explore a data classification problem using a probabilistic ML model for geospatial monitoring, where potentially incorrect decisions could impose severe consequences. To inform our design, we devise a study to investigate data labeling using visualization uncertainty metrics. Following our exploration of visualization for ML-assisted classification, we shift our focus towards the design of user interfaces for high-capacity, generalizable models. We investigate the efficacy of visual guidance in predicting model behavior during image generation tasks, as well as the verification of information synthesized by large language models. In our final work, we look beyond the mechanics of interpretability to explore contextual AI collaboration. We examine how language models provide steerage within exploratory data analysis (EDA) and evaluate the receptiveness of analysts to AI-driven guidance during open-ended discovery. Our work demonstrates that human-AI collaboration depends less on fully exposing the internal mechanics of opaque models than on designing visual and interactive systems that make uncertainty legible, outputs verifiable, and AI guidance actionable within one’s workflow. This work builds upon a multi-disciplinary foundation of machine intelligence, visual perception, and psychology with the aim of mediating the interaction between people and AI.

title: Artificial intelligence based multimodal fusion of electronic medical record data and ECG signals for pericarditis prediction: pericarditis calculator (p-Cal) as a screening aid
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pericarditis may be associated with significant morbidity and mortality and can be a clinically challenging entity to diagnose. There is a clinical need for automated artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms to act as a screening aid to assist with the early and accurate detection of pericarditis. METHODS: We developed p-Cal, a browser-based pericarditis risk calculator that fuses the patient clinical data and 12-lead ECG image to estimate risk for pericarditis. The ECG encoder was designed based on a pretrained MedCLIP Vision Transformer and random forest classifier was used for the clinical tabular data. These two modalities were fused at the decision-level using a meta classifier. Model reasoning for both modalities was assessed using advanced explainable AI techniques-attention maps from the transformer model were used to interpret ECG images, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) force plots were applied to analyse the tabular data. RESULTS: A total of 6508 patients (mean age 54.8±16.1 years, 50.9% female) were used for training and internal validation of the AI model, of whom 902 patients had a confirmed diagnosis of pericarditis (13.8%) and the remainder were normal controls. On 1302 hold-out test patients, the Fusion Model demonstrated the best discriminatory performance, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.89, which surpassed the ECG (AUC = 0.85) and the clinical data only models (AUC = 0.74) performance. On external validation in the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) Database, the fusion model achieved an AUC of 0.81. CONCLUSION: A late fusion AI model integrating tabular clinical electronic medical record data and ECG signal has robust predictive capability for pericarditis as a screening tool.

title: Non-prioritized Kernel Revision
abstract: Abstract Kernel contraction, introduced by Sven Ove Hansson, is a fundamental method for withdrawing information from belief bases. Through the Levi Identity —which defines revision in terms of contraction— kernel contraction also induces the corresponding revision operator known as kernel revision. Recent work has proposed a non-prioritized variant of kernel contraction which, unlike its classical counterpart, may violate the Success postulate, and thereby permits some non-tautological beliefs to be protected from removal. This article develops a corresponding notion of non-prioritized kernel revision. Building on the machinery of classical kernel revision and non-prioritized kernel contraction, we define a revision mechanism that need not always incorporate incoming evidence. The proposal is given both a constructive formulation, via a generalized Levi Identity, and an axiomatic (postulational) characterization. Finally, we analyse its epistemic impact by showing how non-prioritized kernel revision can weaken or reinforce the degree of firmness of selected beliefs within a belief base, and how these effects can accumulate under iteration, eventually yielding endorsement of the epistemic input and de-endorsement of its negation.

title: Prompt-Conditioned Channel Attention for Hierarchical Feature Modulation toward Anatomy-Agnostic Segmentation
abstract: Anatomically plausible segmentation remains challenging because of low contrast, ambiguous boundaries, and modality-specific artifacts. Interactive segmentation has emerged as a promising strategy to guide feature extraction and improve localization, particularly in structurally ambiguous regions. However, existing methods integrate prompts through late-stage fusion and lack explicit mechanisms for prompt-driven channel-wise modulation across hierarchical feature representations, limiting their ability to capture deeper contextual and modality-specific variations. To address these limitations, we introduce Prompt-Conditioned Channel Attention (PCCA), a novel modulation mechanism that enables deep, hierarchical integration of semantic prompts within encoder-decoder networks. PCCA extracts compact channel descriptors via pooling, projects them into a shared space, and fuses them through a gated excitation mechanism to compute prompt-aware channel attention weights. These weights adaptively recalibrate feature responses across multiple network stages, enabling prompt-conditioned, semantically enriched hierarchical representations. Building on this, we propose PROMISE-Net, instantiated in two network variants: a convolutional model (PROMISE-CNN) and a transformer-based model (PROMISE-Txformer). Across the ISIC-Lesion, Kvasir-Polyp, CAMUS-Cardiac, and Kvasir-Instrument benchmarks, integrating PCCA into PROMISE-CNN yielded relative IoU gains of 10.4%, 8.7%, 0.8%, and 3.4%, respectively, over the baseline U-Net, while PROMISE-Txformer achieved corresponding gains of 7.6%, 23.0%, 2.1%, and 1.1%, respectively, over the baseline UNETR. These results show consistent improvements across architectures, imaging modalities, and anatomical targets, establishing PCCA and PROMISE-Net as a scalable, generalizable framework for prompt-aware hierarchical feature modulation in medical image segmentation.

title: Spike-based Belief Propagation in Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
abstract: This paper presents a Bayesian control framework that integrates spike-based dynamics with probabilistic inference for adaptive control. Bayesian inference is widely regarded as a core computational principle of brain function, providing a normative framework for perception, decision-making, and learning under uncertainty. By combining a biologically inspired spiking neural model with Bayesian inference principles, we propose a brain-like control algorithm capable of operating in uncertain environments. We use the mountain car parking problem as a benchmark with non-linear dynamics. Our results demonstrate that the proposed controller can successfully update states in real time and generate goal-directed action plans through spike-driven dynamics. The results highlight the proposed model's potential as a bridge between computational neuroscience and probabilistic control theory.

evidence.title: Spike-based Belief Propagation in Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
evidence.abstract: This paper presents a Bayesian control framework that integrates spike-based dynamics with probabilistic inference for adaptive control. Bayesian inference is widely regarded as a core computational principle of brain function, providing a normative framework for perception, decision-making, and learning under uncertainty. By combining a biologically inspired spiking neural model with Bayesian inference principles, we propose a brain-like control algorithm capable of operating in uncertain environments. We use the mountain car parking problem as a benchmark with non-linear dynamics. Our results demonstrate that the proposed controller can successfully update states in real time and generate goal-directed action plans through spike-driven dynamics. The results highlight the proposed model's potential as a bridge between computational neuroscience and probabilistic control theory.

title: New upper and lower bounds on covering codes K_q(n,R) for alphabets of size 5 <= q <= 21
abstract: Let K_q(n,R) denote the minimum cardinality of a q-ary code of length n with covering radius R. We improve the known bounds on K_q(n,R) in 83 cases (82 distinct cells). On the upper-bound side we give 25 improved bounds for 5<=q<=15 -- twenty-four found by search and one propagated by monotonicity -- using two complementary methods: an engineered focused local search seeded with structural constructions, and a large-neighbourhood search driven by exact full-space coverage transforms that evaluates every candidate codeword position simultaneously. These are, to our knowledge, the first improvements to any upper bound on K_q(n,R) with q >= 5 since the 2011 revision of Keri's tables; several bounds decrease by more than 20%, e.g. K_6(8,4)<=166 (previously 216) and K_8(10,5)<=1883 (previously 2461). On the lower-bound side we give 58 improved bounds for 6<=q<=21, obtained from the semidefinite programming hierarchy of Gijswijt and Polak, whose published results cover q<=5, by combining an exact-arithmetic reimplementation of the reduced program with a multiprecision solution pipeline. Every new lower bound is certified by a rational dual solution validated by a standalone exact-arithmetic checker; no floating-point computation is part of the trusted base. The same pipeline also gives strong numerical evidence of limits: on a dozen further cells the certified value of the relaxation, which the solver reports as optimal to within its working precision, lies below the best known bound, indicating that no improvement is available there at this level of the hierarchy. One cell is improved from both sides: 441<=K_6(10,4)<=2751, previously 417--2952. All codes and certificates are provided in machine-readable form together with standalone verifiers.

title: PL-NBA: A Possession-level Universal Basketball Video Dataset Supporting Multiple Visual Understanding Tasks
abstract: Visual understanding in sports has emerged as a hot topic in computer vision in recent years. Most existing basketball video datasets adopt single action or activity as sample, which can neither preserve the temporal continuity of game events nor support complex tasks such as action anticipation. To address this issue, this paper constructs the first possession-level basketball video dataset (PL-NBA), in which each sample is composed of a complete NBA offensive possession. Collected from 60 NBA games, PL-NBA contains 11,000 valid offensive possession clips and 31,567 annotated events with player names, captions, event types and timestamps. Each video clip includes multiple events and preserves the continuity of events, which is helpful for analysis of tactic. Experiment is conducted on multiple visual understanding tasks, including event recognition, video captioning, temporal action localization and action anticipation. Experimental results show that existing methods achieve limited performance on above four tasks, demonstrating that PL-NBA is a challenging benchmark for sports video understanding.

title: Instruction-Guided Adaptive RAG Evaluation Benchmark
abstract: This dataset records the experimental dataset corresponding to the paper "IG-RAG: Retrieval Enhancement Generation Method Integrating Difficulty Aware Retrieval and Instruction Guided Evidence Utilization". Including the main result data of the paper experiment; Six publicly available datasets used: SQuAD, Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA; Prompt words corresponding to the dataset; A dataset of 60000 self synthesized inference trajectories. And representative complex query examples were carefully selected from general and domain Q&A scenarios, and structured queries were expanded by combining different task instruction constraints. High precision retrievers were used to match multi granularity related document paragraphs, and finally, a processed dataset containing 500 entries was generated through quality filtering and cross validation, ensuring the authority and high accuracy of each data entry.

title: Specialisation Loss: Avoidable Classical Dependence from Correctly-Stated Lemmas
abstract: norm_num closes (2 : ℤ) ≤ 4 through Classical.choice. decide and simp close the same goal without it, and norm_num closes (2 : ℤ) + 2 = 4 without it. The dependence enters through lt_or_eq_of_le : a ≤ b → a < b ∨ a = b, which is stated for a general PartialOrder where equality is not decidable and whose appeal to a classical instance is therefore correct. Nothing in that chain is a mistake. This paper is about that class of defect: a general lemma, correct as written, invoked by a caller that already carries the stronger hypothesis the specialised form would need, and never uses it. Call it specialisation loss. It is distinct from a procedure naming a classical instance outright, and it is harder to repair, because there is no incorrect line to point at. The claim of the paper is that specialisation loss is a cross-system phenomenon rather than a fact about one tactic. It is exhibited in Lean, where norm_num inherits classicality from an order lemma; and in Metamath's set.mm, where four separate proofs establish that a set is finite or countable and then invoke a lemma stated for an arbitrary domain — imadomg where imafi applies, fodomg where fodomfi applies, abrexdom2jm where abrexct applies, and fnrndomg where the well-orderable form does. In two of the four the required fact was proved by the same proof, hundreds of steps earlier, and discarded. The instances in set.mm were repaired and submitted to that library, so the diagnosis is testable rather than interpretive. Dominator analysis supplies the quantity: the order-lemma cluster norm_num routes through is uniquely responsible for 2,018 Mathlib theorems, and the four set.mm repairs free 38, 29, 12 and 9 respectively — figures that deliberately are not added, for reasons §4 sets out.

title: Universal Theory of Computational Identity
abstract: This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework, the Universal Theory of Computational Identity (UTCI), aiming to address the fundamental question of what constitutes a "same computation." Traditional approaches to program equivalence often focus on implementation details, behavioral similarities, or formal semantics. UTCI elevates this inquiry to a higher level, proposing that the core object of study is the 'identity structure' (denoted as `\mathfrak I(C)`) of a computational object – its persistent characteristics regardless of transformations. The theory outlines several key theorems, including the Identity Invariance, Separation, Impossibility, and Canonicalization theorems, along with a central distinction between implementation, behavior, and identity. UTCI moves beyond current program equivalence methodologies by focusing on the inherent nature of computation itself, potentially establishing a foundational framework for future research in areas such as artificial intelligence, formal verification, and distributed systems.

title: Algorithmic Atomicity Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Algorithmic Atomicity Theory (AAT), a novel framework for understanding computation beyond the traditional CPU instruction level. AAT posits that true "atomicity" in computation isn't solely defined by the smallest executable unit, but rather by whether an operation can be further decomposed without sacrificing its inherent computational property. The core question addressed is whether genuine atomic operations exist within the broader landscape of algorithms. This theory shifts the focus from the engineering constraints of hardware (CPU instructions) to a semantic analysis of computational processes, offering a potentially more fundamental understanding of how computation operates at its core. The paper outlines the theoretical foundations of AAT, proposes a formal definition of algorithmic atomicity, and discusses implications for diverse areas of computer science, including parallel computing, quantum computing, and artificial intelligence. ---

title: Universal Computational Adaptation (UCA)
abstract: This paper introduces the Universal Computational Adaptation (UCA) theory, a framework proposing that all computational processes, irrespective of their specific application (e.g., machine learning, database management, data compression, search algorithms), ultimately converge towards a fundamental goal: adaptation to their environment. The core principle of UCA is that any system, regardless of its apparent complexity or purpose, employs underlying mechanisms of sorting, representation, and interpretation to optimize its performance within a given context. We explore the common threads linking seemingly disparate computational paradigms through the lens of this adaptive framework. Specifically, we examine how sorting algorithms, database indexing schemes, compression techniques, and search strategies can be viewed as distinct manifestations of a universal adaptation process, characterized by the minimization of information entropy and the maximization of relevant signal-to-noise ratios. This theory offers a novel perspective on computational design and potentially provides a basis for creating more robust and adaptable systems.

title: AI-Driven Digitization of Marathi Indian Knowledge Systems: A Conceptual Framework for Sustainable and Holistic Development
abstract: Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS), which integrate philosophy, science, ecology, and holistic well-being, comprise an extensive collection of traditional wisdom developed over centuries in the Indian subcontinent.A significant portion of this knowledge is preserved in unstructured textual formats, such as manuscripts, traditional literature, and oral documentation, and is found in regional languages like Marathi.Much of this knowledge is still unavailable in the digital age due to a lack of systematic digitization and computational processing.Computational frameworks that can organize, extract, and interpret original knowledge are therefore becoming increasingly necessary.This paper presents a conceptual AI-driven framework for digitizing and organizing Indian Knowledge Systems found in Marathi.The framework includes text preprocessing, morphological analysis, Named Entity Recognition (NER), Multiword Expression (MWE) detection, semantic concept extraction, and thematic clustering.These NLP techniques enable automatic identification and arrangement of knowledge about sustainability, ethics, ecology, and community-based development.The suggested model places a strong emphasis on combining modern AI technologies with knowledge structures that originate in culture.The framework offers a scalable method for creating digital archives of traditional knowledge by permitting semantic interpretation and knowledge representation of Marathi texts.Initiatives for sustainable development, education, research, and cultural preservation can all benefit from such repositories.By offering a conceptual architecture for maintaining and restoring traditional knowledge systems through computational techniques, the study adds to the growing integration of artificial intelligence and original knowledge digitization.

title: Jamming Extensions of Quantum Correlations Lead to Hidden Superluminal Signaling
abstract: Relativistic causality in certain spacetime configurations permits jamming - superluminal causal influences that nevertheless do not enable superluminal signaling. We fully characterize the correlations compatible with relativistic causality (RC) by extending the operator framework of PRL 104, 140404. When the underlying state is required to be quantum, we prove that any nontrivial jamming - whether state-independent or state-dependent - necessarily leads to hidden superluminal signaling. Thus, the only consistent possibilities are standard quantum correlations without jamming or the full relativistically causal correlation set, with intermediate jamming extensions of quantum correlations leading to signaling. As an application of our characterization, we investigate the security of device-independent (DI) cryptographic primitives against adversaries constrained only by relativistic causality. We construct explicit RC attacks that break DI bit commitment and DI secret sharing in jamming geometries, even when these protocols remain secure against no-signaling adversaries. Our results show that security against relativistic adversaries requires behaviors to be specified together with the spacetime locations of their measurement events; input-output statistics alone are insufficient.

title: Gravitational-wave parameter estimation with machine-learning generated surrogate waveforms
abstract: The worldwide network of gravitational-wave detectors have detected more than 350 binary coalescence events till date. Future third-generation detectors, like Einstein telescope, are expected to detect orders-of-magnitude more signals from sources with more complicated characteristics, including eccentric orbits and high-mass ratio binaries. It is well-established that the computational cost of parameter estimation for signals from these kinds of sources will be extremely high. In particular, the process could be sped-up if generating theoretical waveform predictions, used for likelihood calculation becomes faster. Recently, various machine-learning techniques has been proposed to this end. In this work, we propose a two-stage deterministic conditional-autoencoder model for generating four-parameter SEOBNRv4 waveforms. The first-stage of the model generates amplitude and phase series of the waveform, while the second-stage calibrates the residual error in the predictions. Our model achieves a median mismatch of around $10^{-2}$ with the target polarization waveforms, while the calibrated amplitude/phase series achieve $10^{-6}$ level cosine distance error. We then propose a waveform conditioning step to enable use of these surrogate waveforms for downstream parameter estimation tasks. Finally, we perform extensive parameter estimation tests, with ML and EOB waveform injections and try to recover posterior estimates for the source parameters. We find that when ML waveforms are used to recover EOB target parameter estimates, the inferred posterior have some systematic bias. This inherent bias can be estimated and corrected for, and then importance reweighting of posterior samples can enable use of low-accuracy surrogate waveforms at low SNRs.

title: PETA:Parameter-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation for Virtual Screening
abstract: Accurately ranking active ligands for a target protein pocket from massive chemical libraries remains a central challenge in virtual screening. DrugCLIP and its recent extensions substantially accelerate this process by encoding protein pockets and molecules into a shared embedding space. Despite this progress, further performance improvements typically require retraining the entire model, incurring substantial computational overhead and making target-specific customization inefficient. In this work, we formulate the specialization of pretrained virtual screening models to individual pockets as a test-time adaptation problem and propose PETA, a parameter-efficient framework that directly adapts pretrained model at test time. Given a target pocket, PETA constructs pocket-specific negatives through molecular diffusion and chemical validity filtering, and further moves them toward the reference ligand retrieved from structural databases via embedding-space mixup to create more challenging ranking tasks. A ranking objective then places greater emphasis on suppressing high-scoring invalid candidates that could contaminate the top-ranked screening results, providing structured supervision for lightweight adaptation. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that this lightweight, pocket-specific adaptation outperforms both pretrained and fully retrained baselines while updating only the LayerNorm parameters, which account for approximately $0.03\%$ of the full model.

title: Calibrated Residual-Stream Separability in Modular-Addition Grokking: Complete Result Archive
abstract: Complete result archive for the paper "Calibrated Residual-Stream Interventions Reveal Partial but Not Strong Train–Test Separation in Modular-Addition Grokking." Contains the full per-run outputs of the calibrated low-rank separability search across two canonical settings (p=97/1-layer and p=113/2-layer, five seeds each, seven phases per seed) plus the frozen synthetic calibration: learned projection bases, candidate optimization histories, selected/control/capacity records, rank-64 stress tests, Fourier selected-span diagnostics, checkpoint and split checksums, manifests, and derived summary tables and figures (9,864 files, ~2.3 GiB uncompressed). These are the heavy artifacts excluded from the code repository; lightweight summaries and all generation code are at https://github.com/benchaddha/modular-addition-grokking. Licensed under MIT.

title: Computational Potential Barrier
abstract: This paper explores the concept of a computational potential barrier within the context of optimization problems, particularly those involving complex, multi-dimensional search spaces. The core idea revolves around the inherent difficulty in traversing a landscape where the optimal solution is not immediately accessible, even if a globally better solution exists. We introduce a formal definition of the computational potential barrier, denoted as *BV(x,y)*, which quantifies the minimum energy required to transition from state *x* to state *y* along any possible path. This barrier is defined as the maximum difference in potential between any point *z* along the path and the initial state *x*. The paper highlights the theoretical possibility of achieving optimal solutions through rigorous computation, while simultaneously acknowledging the inevitable presence of computational potential barriers that significantly impact the efficiency and feasibility of such computations. We discuss the factors contributing to these barriers, including the complexity of the objective function, the dimensionality of the search space, and the limitations of available computational resources. The focus is on providing a foundational understanding of this concept, setting the stage for further research into methods for mitigating and overcoming computational potential barriers in diverse applications.

title: Computational Symmetry Index
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Symmetry Index (CSI), a novel metric designed to quantify the inherent symmetry within an algorithm's structure. The core principle is that algorithms with higher symmetry are inherently more amenable to generalization, exhibiting greater robustness across varying input distributions. Conversely, algorithms with low CSI values demonstrate a strong reliance on specific structural characteristics, making them prone to failure when these characteristics are altered. The CSI is defined as the ratio of the number of symmetric elements within an algorithm's representation to the total number of elements. This paper details the formulation of the CSI, explores its theoretical underpinnings, and discusses its potential applications in algorithm design, optimization, and verification. The metric provides a tangible measure for evaluating algorithm design choices and assessing the potential for successful adaptation to novel scenarios.

title: LF-DT: Lumbar Fusion Digital Twin — analysis code and aggregate result tables
abstract: Analysis code and aggregate result tables for the Lumbar Fusion Digital Twin (LF-DT), an electronic health record–based framework that couples calibrated multi-outcome prediction with g-computation re-simulation of alternative lumbar-fusion operative decisions. The repository contains the outcome-channel panel, the counterfactual (what-if) engine, the independently constructed doubly robust augmented inverse-probability-weighted (AIPW) benchmark, negative-control and face-validity analyses, and the code that generates every aggregate table reported in the accompanying manuscript. No patient-level data are included. The repository contains no patient records, patient-level identifiers, temporal-holdout assignments, trained model objects, or individual predicted risks. Aggregate cell counts below 11 are masked. The underlying data were obtained from the TriNetX federated health research network and are available only to investigators at subscribing institutions under a license agreement.
